scope: PostgreSQL extended question bank grounded in the official PostgreSQL 18.6 manual (postgresql.org/docs/18). Original paraphrased content; provenance in source_refs per question.

concepts.description: Identifiers, keywords, constants, dollar quoting and operator structure of PostgreSQL statements.
learning_objectives: Identify the lexical elements that make up a PostgreSQL SQL statement.
Distinguish quoted identifiers from string constants in PostgreSQL syntax.
Use dollar quoting to embed multi-line or quote-heavy text safely.
Explain how operator tokens and comments are recognized by the parser.

concepts.description: Column references, positional parameters, operator invocation, row constructors and expression evaluation.
learning_objectives: Construct value expressions from column references, literals and operators.
Use positional parameters and row constructors correctly in expressions.
Explain how operator precedence and type resolution affect expression evaluation.
Predict the result type of a compound value expression.

concepts.description: Projection items, *, expressions in the select list and output column naming.
learning_objectives: Project columns and expressions in a select list.
Assign aliases that determine output column labels.
Compare SELECT * with an explicit projection and explain its stability.
Explain how PostgreSQL resolves duplicate output column names.

concepts.description: Sorting result rows with ORDER BY, NULLS FIRST/LAST and collation-aware ordering.
learning_objectives: Sort rows with ORDER BY on one or more sort keys.
Place nulls explicitly with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.
Explain how a collation changes the ordering of text values.
Recognize that a query without ORDER BY does not guarantee row order.

concepts.description: Bounded result retrieval with LIMIT/OFFSET and the standard FETCH syntax.
learning_objectives: Restrict a result to the first N rows with LIMIT.
Skip rows with OFFSET for simple pagination.
Use the standard FETCH FIRST syntax as an alternative to LIMIT.
Explain why LIMIT is unstable without a deterministic ORDER BY.

concepts.description: Duplicate removal with DISTINCT and PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON.
learning_objectives: Remove duplicate result rows with DISTINCT.
Use DISTINCT ON to keep one row per key.
Predict how NULL values are treated by duplicate removal.
Explain the sort cost that DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON can introduce.

concepts.description: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and their ALL variants over compatible queries.
learning_objectives: Combine result sets with UNION and UNION ALL.
Use INTERSECT and EXCEPT to compare two result sets.
Ensure matching column counts and compatible types across set operations.
Explain how the ALL variants change duplicate handling.

concepts.description: WITH clauses that define auxiliary statements for a larger query.
learning_objectives: Define a common table expression with a WITH clause.
Use a CTE to structure a complex query into readable stages.
Explain when PostgreSQL may materialize or inline a common table expression.
Compare a CTE with an equivalent subquery or view.

concepts.description: WITH RECURSIVE iteration, termination, search order and cycle handling.
learning_objectives: Write a recursive CTE with a base case and a recursive term.
Design a termination condition that prevents infinite recursion.
Use the SEARCH and CYCLE clauses where hierarchy traversal requires them.
Explain how iteration depth affects recursive query cost.

concepts.description: OVER, PARTITION BY, window frames and ranking/offset window functions.
learning_objectives: Apply a window function over a partition without collapsing rows.
Define a window frame for a window aggregate calculation.
Use ranking functions to number rows within partitions.
Distinguish window functions from GROUP BY aggregation.

concepts.description: CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, GREATEST and LEAST.
learning_objectives: Write searched and simple CASE expressions.
Replace NULL with COALESCE or convert it with NULLIF.
Choose between GREATEST/LEAST and CASE for value selection.
Explain the result type rules that apply to a CASE expression.

concepts.description: NULL semantics, IS NULL/IS DISTINCT FROM and how AND/OR/NOT treat unknown.
learning_objectives: Explain how SQL three-valued logic treats the unknown truth value.
Test for NULL with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.
Use IS DISTINCT FROM for NULL-safe comparison.
Predict the result of AND, OR and NOT when an operand is unknown.

concepts.description: Set-valued aggregates, FILTER, ORDER BY inside aggregates and grouping sets.
learning_objectives: Summarize rows with aggregate functions.
Filter aggregate input rows with the FILTER clause.
Use grouping sets, ROLLUP or CUBE for multi-level summaries.
Distinguish COUNT(*) from COUNT(column) when NULL values are present.

concepts.description: Inner, outer, cross, natural and LATERAL join semantics.
learning_objectives: Select the join variant that preserves the required rows.
Write a CROSS JOIN and explain its row count.
Use LATERAL to reference preceding FROM items.
Explain the risks of NATURAL joins in evolving schemas.

concepts.description: Integer, arbitrary-precision numeric and floating-point types, serial and arithmetic behavior.
learning_objectives: Choose between integer, numeric and floating-point types for a value.
Explain the precision and rounding behavior of numeric versus floating point.
Recognize integer overflow and integer division semantics.
Explain the storage and range differences among integer widths.

concepts.description: character varying, character and text, padding and length semantics.
learning_objectives: Choose between varchar, char and text for a column.
Explain blank padding in fixed-length character values.
Enforce or avoid length limits with a length modifier.
Predict comparison behavior across the character types.

concepts.description: boolean storage, accepted literals and NULL truth values.
learning_objectives: Store and query boolean values with the accepted literals.
Predict how NULL affects boolean truth values.
Use a boolean expression directly as a WHERE condition.
Compare boolean columns without redundant equality tests.

concepts.description: date, time, timestamp with/without time zone and interval.
learning_objectives: Choose between date, time and timestamp types.
Explain the difference between timestamp and timestamptz.
Perform interval arithmetic on date/time values.
Predict how the session time zone affects displayed timestamps.

concepts.description: json versus jsonb storage semantics, containment, indexing and subscripting.
learning_objectives: Compare json and jsonb storage and performance characteristics.
Query JSON values with operators and path expressions.
Test containment and key existence with jsonb operators.
Decide when JSON storage should be normalized into relational columns.

concepts.description: Array declaration, literals, indexing, slicing and searching.
learning_objectives: Declare and populate array columns.
Access elements and slices with array subscripts.
Search arrays with ANY, ALL and array operators.
Expand an array into rows with unnest.

concepts.description: Enumerated types, UUID, XML, network and bit-string types.
learning_objectives: Choose an enumerated type for a fixed value set.
Generate and store UUID values.
Use network and bit-string types for their intended data.
Explain the tradeoffs of enum types when the allowed values change.

concepts.description: Built-in ranges, bounds, overlap and construction.
learning_objectives: Construct range values with explicit bounds.
Test whether ranges contain, overlap or are adjacent to one another.
Choose an index strategy for range queries.
Explain how a multirange collects disjoint range values.

concepts.description: Cast syntax, implicit/assignment/explicit casts and union type resolution.
learning_objectives: Cast values explicitly with CAST and the :: syntax.
Distinguish implicit, assignment and explicit cast contexts.
Predict type resolution for operators and UNION branches.
Explain when an explicit cast is required to avoid ambiguity.

concepts.description: Collation-aware ordering and comparison, COLLATE clauses and ICU.
learning_objectives: Explain how a collation determines text ordering and comparison.
Apply COLLATE to a column or expression.
Distinguish deterministic from nondeterministic collations.
Diagnose ordering differences caused by a database or column collation.

concepts.description: Domains as base types with reusable CHECK constraints.
learning_objectives: Define a domain over a base type with constraints.
Reuse a domain to enforce a consistent business rule.
Explain how domain constraints interact with column constraints.
Decide when a domain is preferable to a plain constrained column.

concepts.description: String operators and functions such as concatenation, substring and trim.
learning_objectives: Combine text with concatenation operators and functions.
Extract substrings and trim unwanted characters.
Replace and search text with built-in functions.
Predict NULL propagation in string expressions.

concepts.description: Numeric operators and functions such as round, trunc, mod and random.
learning_objectives: Round and truncate numeric values with the correct function.
Compute remainders and powers with numeric operators.
Generate pseudo-random values and explain their limitations.
Predict the numeric result type and rounding behavior of a function.

concepts.description: current_date/now, extract, date_trunc, age and interval arithmetic.
learning_objectives: Obtain the current date and timestamp with the built-in functions.
Extract fields from date/time values with EXTRACT.
Truncate timestamps to a chosen granularity.
Compute elapsed time with interval arithmetic.

concepts.description: LIKE, ILIKE, SIMILAR TO and POSIX regular expressions.
learning_objectives: Match text with LIKE and ILIKE patterns.
Choose SIMILAR TO or a POSIX regular expression for complex patterns.
Escape wildcard characters in literal search terms.
Explain the performance risk of patterns that begin with a wildcard.

concepts.description: tsvector/tsquery, matching @@, ranking and FTS indexing.
learning_objectives: Convert documents and queries to tsvector and tsquery.
Match documents with the @@ operator.
Rank results by relevance.
Design an index that supports full-text search.

concepts.description: CREATE TABLE, column defaults, temporary and unlogged tables.
learning_objectives: Create a table with columns, data types and defaults.
Choose temporary or unlogged tables for appropriate use cases.
Explain the lifecycle and visibility of temporary tables.
Predict the storage and durability implications of unlogged tables.

concepts.description: GENERATED ALWAYS/BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY versus serial.
learning_objectives: Define an identity column with ALWAYS or BY DEFAULT.
Compare identity columns with legacy serial columns.
Explain how identity generation interacts with explicit inserts.
Identify the sequence object behind a generated key.

concepts.description: Stored generated columns, expression rules and restrictions.
learning_objectives: Define a stored generated column with an expression.
Explain why only immutable expressions are allowed.
Compare generated columns with views and triggers.
Predict when the stored generated value is recomputed.

concepts.description: CHECK, NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraint semantics.
learning_objectives: Enforce row-level rules with CHECK and NOT NULL constraints.
Prevent duplicate values with UNIQUE constraints.
Explain how NULL values interact with UNIQUE and CHECK.
Test a constraint with both valid and invalid rows.

concepts.description: Key declaration, referential actions and deferred enforcement.
learning_objectives: Declare primary and foreign keys for related tables.
Choose a referential action for deletes and updates.
Explain deferred constraint checking inside a transaction.
Diagnose foreign-key violations caused by insertion order.

concepts.description: ALTER TABLE operations and their effects.
learning_objectives: Add, alter and drop columns with ALTER TABLE.
Predict when an ALTER TABLE operation rewrites or locks a table.
Change constraints and defaults on an existing table.
Plan a schema change that preserves existing data.

concepts.description: Schema organization, name resolution and the public schema.
learning_objectives: Create schemas to group related database objects.
Resolve unqualified object names through search_path.
Explain the security implications of the public schema.
Qualify objects explicitly when names could be ambiguous.

concepts.description: View semantics, updatable views and CHECK OPTION.
learning_objectives: Define a view over a query.
Query a view as if it were a table.
Explain which views are automatically updatable.
Use WITH CHECK OPTION to constrain modifications made through a view.

concepts.description: Materialized view storage, refresh and when to prefer them.
learning_objectives: Create and populate a materialized view.
Refresh a materialized view and explain why its data can be stale.
Compare materialized views with ordinary views.
Decide when a materialized view is worth its storage cost.

concepts.description: Declarative range/list/hash partitioning, pruning and defaults.
learning_objectives: Choose a partitioning strategy for a large table.
Create partitions and a default partition.
Explain partition pruning during query planning.
Recognize the limitations of partitioned tables.

concepts.description: Data modification statements, ON CONFLICT and RETURNING.
learning_objectives: Insert, update and delete rows with the data modification statements.
Return modified rows with the RETURNING clause.
Resolve conflicts with ON CONFLICT.
Predict the rows affected by an UPDATE or DELETE predicate.

concepts.description: Conditional merge of a source table into a target.
learning_objectives: Write a MERGE statement with matched and unmatched branches.
Choose WHEN MATCHED actions for updates or deletes.
Compare MERGE with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT.
Predict MERGE behavior when the source contains duplicate keys.

concepts.description: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, atomicity, savepoints and transaction properties.
learning_objectives: Group statements into an atomic transaction.
Roll back work with ROLLBACK or a savepoint.
Explain the atomicity and durability guarantees of a committed transaction.
Recognize operations that cannot run inside a transaction block.

concepts.description: Read committed, repeatable read and serializable behavior in PostgreSQL.
learning_objectives: Compare the isolation levels that PostgreSQL supports.
Explain which concurrency anomalies each isolation level prevents.
Recognize a serialization failure and retry the transaction safely.
Choose an isolation level for a concurrent workload.

concepts.description: Multiversion snapshots, visibility and their consequences.
learning_objectives: Explain how PostgreSQL keeps multiple row versions.
Describe how a snapshot determines row visibility.
Relate dead tuples to the vacuum requirement.
Predict why readers and writers generally do not block each other under MVCC.

concepts.description: Table/row locks, FOR UPDATE/SHARE, deadlocks and advisory locks.
learning_objectives: Acquire row locks with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE.
Explain how consistent lock ordering prevents deadlocks.
Read a deadlock error and choose a retry strategy.
Use advisory locks for application-level coordination.

concepts.description: Index purpose, cost, unique/partial/expression and multicolumn indexes.
learning_objectives: Explain how an index accelerates selective access.
Create partial, expression and multicolumn indexes.
Choose the column order for a multicolumn index.
Recognize the write cost of maintaining an index.

concepts.description: B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN selection.
learning_objectives: Match each index type to the data and operators it supports.
Explain when a GIN index is appropriate.
Use a BRIN index for a large, naturally ordered table.
Compare the storage and lookup tradeoffs of the index types.

concepts.description: Reading plan trees, cost estimates, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and scan types.
learning_objectives: Read a query plan tree from the innermost node outward.
Compare estimated cost with actual execution time.
Identify sequential, index and bitmap scans in a plan.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to diagnose a slow query.

concepts.description: ANALYZE statistics, selectivity and statistics targets.
learning_objectives: Explain how table and column statistics guide the query planner.
Run ANALYZE and interpret its effect on a plan.
Increase the statistics target for a skewed column.
Recognize plan changes caused by stale statistics.

concepts.description: Role attributes, INHERIT, group roles and SET ROLE.
learning_objectives: Create a role with or without login capability.
Grant role membership and explain privilege inheritance.
Use SET ROLE to act with another role's privileges.
Avoid sharing a superuser role for ordinary application access.

concepts.description: GRANT/REVOKE, object privileges and grant options.
learning_objectives: Grant and revoke privileges on database objects.
Explain which privileges a role needs to complete a task.
Use WITH GRANT OPTION and explain its risk.
Audit the effective privileges of a role.

concepts.description: Policies, USING/WITH CHECK, permissive vs restrictive and bypass rules.
learning_objectives: Enable row-level security on a table.
Write USING and WITH CHECK policies for access control.
Explain how permissive and restrictive policies combine.
Identify the roles that bypass row-level security.

concepts.description: CREATE FUNCTION, arguments, volatility categories and SETOF results.
learning_objectives: Define a function with typed arguments and a return type.
Choose the correct volatility category for a function.
Return a set of rows with SETOF.
Explain how volatility affects planner behavior.

concepts.description: Blocks, declarations, control structures, statements and exceptions.
learning_objectives: Structure a PL/pgSQL program with declaration and body blocks.
Use IF/ELSIF and loop constructs for control flow.
Declare and assign variables inside a PL/pgSQL function.
Handle errors with EXCEPTION blocks.

concepts.description: CREATE PROCEDURE, CALL and transaction control in procedures.
learning_objectives: Create and invoke a procedure with CREATE PROCEDURE and CALL.
Use transaction control statements inside a procedure.
Distinguish procedures from functions.
Choose a procedure when a task needs multiple transactions.

concepts.description: Trigger timing, row/statement granularity, NEW/OLD and trigger functions.
learning_objectives: Create a trigger that fires before or after a data change.
Choose row-level or statement-level trigger timing.
Access NEW and OLD row values inside a trigger function.
Explain the performance and recursion risks of triggers.

concepts.description: postgresql.conf, ALTER SYSTEM and key resource settings.
learning_objectives: Locate and interpret key PostgreSQL configuration parameters.
Change a setting with ALTER SYSTEM and apply it with reload or restart.
Distinguish session, database and cluster-level settings.
Tune a resource parameter and observe its effect.

concepts.description: VACUUM variants, autovacuum, visibility map and wraparound.
learning_objectives: Explain why dead tuples accumulate and require vacuuming.
Run VACUUM and VACUUM ANALYZE appropriately.
Describe autovacuum's role and triggering conditions.
Recognize transaction ID wraparound risk.

concepts.description: SQL dump, file-system backup, PITR and their tradeoffs.
learning_objectives: Choose between logical dumps and physical backups.
Perform a logical backup with pg_dump and restore it.
Explain how point-in-time recovery uses a base backup and archived WAL.
Verify a backup before relying on it.

concepts.description: WAL purpose, durability and archiving basics.
learning_objectives: Explain why changes are written to WAL before data files.
Describe how checkpoints bound recovery time.
Configure WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery.
Relate WAL settings to durability and write throughput.

concepts.description: Physical vs logical replication, streaming and slots.
learning_objectives: Compare physical and logical replication.
Describe how a standby streams and applies WAL.
Explain the role of replication slots.
Choose a replication approach for a failover or data-distribution requirement.

concepts.description: Cumulative statistics views and activity monitoring.
learning_objectives: Inspect active sessions with pg_stat_activity.
Identify expensive statements using statistics views.
Interpret cumulative statistics for tables and indexes.
Design a monitoring check for a database health condition.

concepts.description: Project columns and computed expressions from a table with SELECT, control duplicate rows and assign readable output column names.
learning_objectives: Project the required columns and expressions in a SELECT list.
Assign readable output names with column aliases.
Remove duplicate result rows with DISTINCT and state the cost of doing so.
Predict the result columns produced by SELECT * and by an explicit column list.

concepts.description: Filter source rows with a boolean WHERE predicate that combines comparison, range, membership and NULL-aware conditions.
learning_objectives: Build a WHERE predicate that keeps exactly the rows required by a specification.
Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT while respecting operator precedence.
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL instead of equality when NULL values are involved.
Explain why a predicate that compares with NULL yields unknown rather than true.

concepts.description: Combine rows from related tables with JOIN, writing correct ON predicates and selecting the join type that matches the required result.
learning_objectives: Translate a relationship between tables into a correct JOIN ... ON condition.
Choose an inner or outer join based on whether unmatched rows must be kept.
Diagnose unexpected duplicate rows caused by a one-to-many join key.
Join three or more tables without losing the intended row population.

concepts.description: Group rows into sets with GROUP BY and compute per-group aggregates such as counts, sums and averages.
learning_objectives: Group rows by one or more columns to produce one output row per group.
Apply aggregate functions to summarize each group.
Distinguish a grouping column from an aggregated expression in the SELECT list.
Explain how a NULL grouping key forms its own group.

concepts.description: Filter grouped results with HAVING, distinguishing group-level predicates from row-level WHERE conditions.
learning_objectives: Apply HAVING to keep only groups that satisfy an aggregate condition.
Choose WHERE for row filtering and HAVING for group filtering inside the same query.
Explain why a WHERE clause cannot reference an aggregate result directly.
Predict the difference in output when a predicate moves from WHERE to HAVING.

concepts.description: Compose queries with scalar, row, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries in the SELECT, FROM and WHERE clauses.
learning_objectives: Use a scalar subquery where a single computed value is required.
Compare IN, EXISTS and join formulations for the same filtering task.
Write a correlated subquery that references the current outer row.
Explain when a subquery in FROM acts as an independent derived table.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which statement about unquoted identifiers is correct?

options.option_text: They are case sensitive and always stored exactly as written
They are folded to lower case, so Orders, ORDERS and orders name the same object
They are folded to upper case, so Orders and ORDERS are identical but orders differs

questions.explanation: Unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive because PostgreSQL folds them to lower case. Quoting an identifier preserves case and makes it case-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid way to write a string literal containing an apostrophe in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Inside a standard string literal an apostrophe is escaped by doubling it (''). Double quotes delimit identifiers, not strings.

questions.prompt: What does PostgreSQL's dollar quoting ($$...$$) provide?

options.option_text: A way to write string constants without escaping embedded quotes
A parameterized substitution for prepared statements
A syntax for dollar-amount monetary literals
A comment delimiter for multi-line notes

questions.explanation: Dollar-quoted strings let a function body or long literal contain quote characters directly, avoiding '' escaping.

questions.prompt: A column was created with CREATE TABLE t ("Total" numeric). Why does SELECT total FROM t fail?

options.option_text: Quoted columns are never visible to SELECT
total is a reserved word in PostgreSQL
The column must be referenced with square brackets: [Total]
The unquoted name total folds to lower case, but the stored name is the case-sensitive Total

questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE with the quoted identifier "Total" stores the name with its case preserved. Unquoted total folds to lower case total, which does not match; the query needs "Total".

questions.prompt: In a PostgreSQL expression like 3 + 4 * 2, what determines the result 11?

options.option_text: The order columns appear in the table
PostgreSQL evaluates * and + in input order only when parentheses are present
Operator precedence rules fixed by the parser
Left-to-right evaluation of all operators equally

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL applies standard operator precedence: * binds tighter than +, so 4 * 2 is evaluated first, giving 11.

questions.prompt: What does the row constructor expression ROW(1, 'a') = ROW(1, 'a') evaluate to?

options.option_text: an error: rows cannot be compared

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL compares row constructors element-by-element; equal fields make the whole comparison true.

questions.prompt: SELECT 1 = NULL; returns which value in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Comparison with NULL yields NULL (unknown) rather than true or false; this is standard three-valued logic.

questions.prompt: Which expression selects rows where a is between 5 and 10 inclusive on both ends?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN x AND y is equivalent to a >= x AND a <= y — both bounds are inclusive.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT * FROM t return?

options.option_text: All columns sorted alphabetically by name
All columns of every selected row in the table's defined column order

questions.explanation: * expands to every column of the table(s) in FROM, in declared order.

questions.prompt: In SELECT price * qty AS amount, what does AS amount do?

options.option_text: Creates a stored column named amount

questions.explanation: AS assigns an output column label; the label exists only in the result and can be referenced by ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: A query uses SELECT a + b total FROM t ORDER BY total. Why is this valid?

options.option_text: AS labels create real columns in the table
Output column labels are visible to ORDER BY
ORDER BY re-evaluates a + b automatically
PostgreSQL ignores ORDER BY names that are not real columns

questions.explanation: ORDER BY can reference output column labels assigned with AS in the same SELECT.

questions.prompt: Where can an output column label assigned by AS NOT be used directly?

options.option_text: In the same query's WHERE clause
In a client application reading the result
In the column header of the result

questions.explanation: WHERE is logically evaluated before the select list, so select-list labels are not in scope there; a WHERE must repeat the expression.

questions.prompt: By default, where do NULL values sort in PostgreSQL ORDER BY ... ASC?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL sorts NULLs as larger than any non-null value, so they come last for ASC and first for DESC unless NULLS FIRST/LAST says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which clause forces NULL values to sort before non-NULL values in ascending order?

options.option_text: ORDER BY col ASC WITH NULLS FIRST
ORDER BY col ASC NULLS FIRST
ORDER BY col ASC NULLS LOW

questions.explanation: NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST explicitly control null placement, overriding the default (nulls sort larger than non-nulls).

questions.prompt: ORDER BY 2 refers to what?

options.option_text: The second column in the output select list
The second column physically stored in the table

questions.explanation: ORDER BY accepts output column numbers; 2 means the second select-list item.

questions.prompt: A query orders employees by name. Two installations return different orderings for accented names. What most likely explains this?

options.option_text: ORDER BY is nondeterministic by design
name contains hidden spaces that PostgreSQL randomly reorders
The sort always depends on table size

questions.explanation: Text ordering follows the column's collation; different collation settings produce different orderings for non-ASCII text.

questions.prompt: Which pair returns at most 5 rows, skipping the first 10?
questions.explanation: LIMIT n caps the row count; OFFSET m skips m rows first. PostgreSQL also supports the SQL-standard FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY form.

questions.prompt: Why should a LIMIT query almost always include ORDER BY?

options.option_text: LIMIT is illegal without ORDER BY
Without ORDER BY the set of returned rows is unpredictable
ORDER BY makes LIMIT run faster

questions.explanation: LIMIT only bounds how many rows are returned; which rows arrive is arbitrary unless ORDER BY fixes an ordering.

questions.prompt: What does LIMIT ALL mean in PostgreSQL?

options.option_text: It is equivalent to omitting LIMIT — no row bound is applied
It returns only the first page of rows
It limits rows to the total table size

questions.explanation: LIMIT ALL (or LIMIT NULL) explicitly requests no limit, which PostgreSQL accepts for compatibility.

questions.prompt: SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM employees does what?

options.option_text: Deletes duplicate dept rows from the table
Returns each different dept value once
Returns the first row of each dept with all columns

questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; SELECT DISTINCT dept keeps one row per distinct dept value.

questions.prompt: How does DISTINCT treat NULL values?

options.option_text: All NULLs are considered equal to each other, collapsing to a single row
Each NULL is treated as a distinct value
NULLs are always removed from the result
DISTINCT fails when NULLs are present

questions.explanation: For DISTINCT, NULLs are treated as duplicates of one another — a column of only NULLs yields one row.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept) dept, name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY dept, salary DESC return?

options.option_text: An error: DISTINCT ON requires the select list to match
Every row, sorted by dept then salary
The first row per dept — here, each department's highest-paid employee

questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group defined by its expressions; ORDER BY must lead with those expressions to determine which row is 'first'.

questions.prompt: For DISTINCT ON (dept) to predictably return the newest row per dept, the ORDER BY must start with:

options.option_text: dept, then a descending date column

questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON requires the leftmost ORDER BY expressions to match the DISTINCT ON expressions; remaining keys pick which row survives.

questions.prompt: UNION (without ALL) of two SELECTs produces:

options.option_text: Only rows in the first query absent from the second
The rows of both queries with duplicates removed
All rows of both queries including duplicates
Only rows present in both queries

questions.explanation: UNION computes the set union and eliminates duplicates; UNION ALL keeps duplicates.

questions.prompt: When might UNION ALL be preferable to UNION?

options.option_text: When duplicates are acceptable or impossible — it skips the sort/hash needed for deduplication
When the result must be sorted
When the two queries return different column counts
When NULLs must be preserved (UNION removes them)

questions.explanation: UNION must sort or hash rows to deduplicate; UNION ALL just concatenates results, which is cheaper.

questions.prompt: INTERSECT returns rows that are:

options.option_text: In either query but not both
In the first query but not the second

questions.explanation: INTERSECT is the set intersection; EXCEPT is the set difference (first minus second).

questions.prompt: For two SELECTs combined with UNION to be valid, they must:

options.option_text: Return the same number of columns with pairwise-compatible types

questions.explanation: Set operations require equal column counts and compatible (coercible) data types in each position.

questions.explanation: DEFAULT supplies the value used when INSERT omits the column (or uses DEFAULT keyword).

questions.prompt: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY versus GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY differ in:

options.option_text: ALWAYS rejects user-supplied values (except OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE); BY DEFAULT uses the sequence only when no value is given

questions.explanation: ALWAYS enforces sequence-generated values (overridable only via OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE); BY DEFAULT permits explicit values.

questions.prompt: Why is GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY preferred over serial in modern PostgreSQL?

options.option_text: It is the SQL-standard mechanism with better permission semantics and explicit user-value control

questions.explanation: Identity is standard SQL, uses sequences under the hood, and distinguishes ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT behavior; serial predates it.

questions.prompt: A stored generated column total int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * price) STORED:

options.option_text: Computes qty*price at write time and stores the result

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports STORED generated columns computed on write; they cannot be assigned in INSERT/UPDATE.

questions.prompt: The generation expression of a generated column must be:

options.option_text: Immutable — it may not reference other tables, other generated columns, or volatile functions like now()

questions.explanation: Generation expressions must be immutable and may only use the row's own non-generated columns.

questions.prompt: A NOT NULL constraint enforces:

options.option_text: The column may not contain NULL values

questions.explanation: NOT NULL rejects NULL on insert/update — distinct from UNIQUE, which permits NULLs (multiple, by default).

questions.prompt: CHECK (price > 0) on a column:

options.option_text: Validates every inserted/updated row: the expression must not be false (NULL passes)

questions.explanation: CHECK requires the expression be true or NULL (unknown passes); it is evaluated on each write.

questions.prompt: Under default PostgreSQL semantics, a UNIQUE column allows:

options.option_text: Multiple NULLs — NULLs are treated as not equal

questions.explanation: Standard SQL treats NULLs as distinct for uniqueness; PostgreSQL 15+ offers UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT to change this.

questions.prompt: CHECK constraints that reference other rows or subqueries:

options.option_text: Require a trigger instead of any CHECK
Are not allowed — CHECK may only use immutable expressions on the current row

questions.explanation: CHECK expressions must be immutable and per-row; cross-row rules need triggers or exclusion constraints.

questions.prompt: A PRIMARY KEY in PostgreSQL implicitly creates:

options.option_text: A unique B-tree index and NOT NULL constraints on its columns
A foreign key on the parent table

questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL enforced by a unique index.

questions.prompt: FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(id) ON DELETE CASCADE means:

options.option_text: Deleting a dept row automatically deletes referencing rows

questions.explanation: ON DELETE actions: CASCADE deletes children; SET NULL/DEFAULT resets them; RESTRICT/NO ACTION forbid it.

questions.prompt: ON UPDATE CASCADE on a foreign key does what when the parent's key changes?

options.option_text: Propagates the new key value to all referencing child rows

questions.explanation: CASCADE updates children to follow the parent's changed key — one of the referential actions.

questions.prompt: A DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED foreign key is checked:

options.option_text: At transaction commit, allowing out-of-order inserts within the transaction

questions.explanation: Deferrable constraints postpone enforcement to COMMIT — essential for cyclic references and bulk loads.

questions.prompt: Why must a referenced column set be UNIQUE (or PRIMARY KEY) for a FOREIGN KEY?

options.option_text: Each child row must identify exactly one parent row
Foreign keys need faster lookups only

questions.explanation: An FK must reference a unique column combination so every child maps to at most one parent.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c int DEFAULT 0 on a large existing table:

options.option_text: Is typically fast — PostgreSQL stores the default for existing rows without rewriting the whole table

questions.explanation: Constant/immutable defaults avoid a table rewrite in modern PostgreSQL — existing rows read the catalog default.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a big table generally:

options.option_text: May rewrite the entire table and takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock

questions.explanation: Type changes that alter storage force a rewrite and block concurrent access — a classic migration hazard.

questions.prompt: search_path controls:

options.option_text: Which schemas PostgreSQL searches for unqualified object names
The list of files to back up

questions.explanation: Unqualified names resolve against search_path schemas in order; objects may be created in the first listed schema.

questions.prompt: Two tables can share the same name orders if:
questions.explanation: Schemas are namespaces; sales.orders and audit.orders can coexist.

questions.prompt: Since PostgreSQL 15, default public-schema privileges changed so that:

options.option_text: New databases no longer grant CREATE on public to PUBLIC role by default
Everyone can still create tables in public
public schema is deleted at install

questions.explanation: v15 tightened defaults: public schema creation rights were removed from PUBLIC to reduce surprise writes.

questions.prompt: A view in PostgreSQL is:

options.option_text: A copy of the table made at creation
Only readable, never writable under any circumstances
A stored query that behaves like a virtual table — data lives in the underlying tables

questions.explanation: Views store a query, not data. Materialized views are the stored-result counterpart.

questions.prompt: A simple updatable view (one table, no aggregates) supports INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because:

options.option_text: It requires INSTEAD OF triggers always
PostgreSQL rewrites the modification against the base table

questions.explanation: Automatically-updatable views translate DML to the base relation when rules are met; otherwise INSTEAD OF triggers are needed.

questions.prompt: WITH CHECK OPTION on an updatable view enforces:

options.option_text: Rows written through the view must satisfy the view's WHERE condition

questions.explanation: CHECK OPTION prevents INSERT/UPDATE through the view from producing rows invisible to the view itself.

questions.prompt: A materialized view differs from a regular view in that it:

options.option_text: Stores the query result physically and must be REFRESHed to see new base data

questions.explanation: Materialized views cache results for fast reads at the cost of staleness; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes.

source_refs.section: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW
source_refs.title: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW

questions.prompt: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY:

options.option_text: Locks the view for all readers
Allows reads during refresh but requires a UNIQUE index on the view

questions.explanation: CONCURRENTLY keeps the view readable during refresh (using a unique index for diff application).

source_refs.section: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW

questions.prompt: Declarative partitioning in PostgreSQL is declared via:
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY creates a partitioned parent; children are created AS PARTITION OF with bounds.

questions.prompt: Partition pruning means:

options.option_text: The planner skips partitions that cannot contain rows matching the query's WHERE conditions

questions.explanation: When the partition key appears in the WHERE clause, the planner eliminates non-matching partitions from the scan.

questions.prompt: A DEFAULT partition exists to:

options.option_text: Catch rows that match no declared partition bounds

questions.explanation: Without a default partition, rows outside all defined bounds fail at insert; the default partition absorbs them.

questions.prompt: For declaratively partitioned tables, a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint must:
questions.explanation: Uniqueness is enforced per-partition, so the key must cover the partition columns to guarantee global uniqueness.

questions.prompt: INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4) inserts:

options.option_text: An error — multi-row VALUES needs UNION

questions.explanation: INSERT accepts a comma-separated list of row values.

questions.prompt: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name means:

options.option_text: EXCLUDED refers to the old row
On an email uniqueness violation, update the existing row's name from the proposed row

questions.explanation: EXCLUDED is the row that would have been inserted; ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE applies it to the conflicting existing row (upsert).

questions.prompt: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING:

options.option_text: Skips the insert when a conflict occurs, without error

questions.explanation: DO NOTHING makes an otherwise-failing insert a no-op — the idempotent insert pattern.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM t RETURNING id gives back:

options.option_text: The id of each deleted row in the same statement

questions.explanation: RETURNING works on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE, exposing the affected rows' values (old for DELETE, new for UPDATE).

questions.prompt: UPDATE t SET a = a + 1 FROM other WHERE t.id = other.id uses:

options.option_text: A subquery that must return one row
A FROM clause joining a second table into the update

questions.explanation: UPDATE ... FROM lets another table's columns feed the SET and match rows — PostgreSQL's join-update syntax.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM t USING u WHERE t.id = u.id does:

options.option_text: Deletes t rows matched by rows in u — the join-delete

questions.explanation: USING is to DELETE what FROM is to UPDATE — auxiliary relations for matching.

questions.prompt: MERGE INTO target USING source ON cond WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT:

options.option_text: Conditionally updates or inserts per source row depending on the match

questions.explanation: MERGE (SQL standard, PG 15+) performs matched/not-matched actions combining insert, update, delete in one pass.

questions.prompt: A documented MERGE caveat versus ON CONFLICT upsert is:

options.option_text: MERGE cannot create a unique-constraint race guarantee — concurrent inserts may still violate; ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE handles races atomically
MERGE is always slower with no advantages

questions.explanation: MERGE's source-driven WHEN clauses differ from ON CONFLICT's speculative-insert path; concurrent workloads can still see unique violations.

questions.prompt: A transaction's atomicity guarantee means:

options.option_text: Other users can see partial results
All its statements take effect, or none do

questions.explanation: COMMIT applies everything; ROLLBACK or failure undoes everything — the 'all or nothing' property.

questions.prompt: SAVEPOINT inside a transaction allows:

options.option_text: Rolling back part of the transaction's work while keeping the rest

questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT marks a point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes later work without aborting the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: In autocommit mode (no explicit BEGIN), each statement:

options.option_text: Shares one transaction with all sessions
Runs in its own transaction, committing on success

questions.explanation: Absent BEGIN, PostgreSQL wraps each statement in an implicit transaction.

questions.prompt: After an error mid-transaction (e.g. constraint violation), PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Aborts the transaction — subsequent statements fail until ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT

questions.explanation: An error poisons the transaction ('current transaction is aborted'); only rollback-to-savepoint or full rollback recovers.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is:
questions.explanation: Read Committed is the default; PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed internally.

questions.prompt: Under Read Committed in PostgreSQL, two identical SELECTs in one transaction can return different rows because:

options.option_text: Each statement sees a snapshot taken at statement start

questions.explanation: Read Committed takes a per-statement snapshot — committed changes between statements become visible (non-repeatable read allowed).

questions.prompt: Which phenomena does PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevent?

options.option_text: Dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads — but not serialization anomalies

questions.explanation: PG Repeatable Read uses a transaction-long snapshot, preventing dirty/non-repeatable/phantom; serialization anomalies remain possible.

questions.prompt: Requesting SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED in PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Is accepted but behaves as Read Committed — PostgreSQL has no real Read Uncommitted

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL implements no dirty reads; the standard's minimum guarantee is Read Committed, so it maps to that.

questions.prompt: Serializable isolation in PostgreSQL is implemented by:

options.option_text: Snapshot isolation plus serialization-anomaly detection (SSI) that aborts dangerous transactions

questions.explanation: Serializable Snapshot Isolation tracks rw-antidependencies; transactions forming dangerous structures get serialization failures.

questions.prompt: Under MVCC, readers in PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Do not block writers, and writers do not block readers — each sees a consistent snapshot

questions.explanation: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so each transaction sees a snapshot — reads never wait on row writes and vice versa.

questions.prompt: An UPDATE in PostgreSQL physically:

options.option_text: Creates a new row version; the old version stays until no snapshot can see it
Overwrites the row in place always

questions.explanation: MVCC updates write new tuples; dead tuples accumulate until VACUUM reclaims them — the reason vacuum exists.

questions.prompt: Which statement about visibility is correct?

options.option_text: Uncommitted rows of other transactions are visible at Read Committed
Snapshots refresh each statement at Serializable
A transaction sees its own writes plus rows committed before its snapshot began
A transaction sees all committed rows always

questions.explanation: Visibility = snapshot at begin (per-transaction or per-statement) + own writes; others' in-flight work stays invisible.

questions.prompt: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE does what?

options.option_text: Locks the selected rows against concurrent updates/deletes until the transaction ends

questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE takes row-level write locks (like a DELETE would) — the read-modify-write pattern's locking primitive.

questions.prompt: A deadlock occurs when:

options.option_text: Two transactions each hold locks the other needs — PostgreSQL detects this and aborts one

questions.explanation: Deadlock detector (deadlock_timeout) finds lock cycles and cancels one participant with a deadlock error.

questions.prompt: SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE versus FOR UPDATE:

options.option_text: NO KEY means no lock is taken
FOR NO KEY UPDATE is weaker — it doesn't block changes to non-key columns by other lockers

questions.explanation: Lock strengths: FOR KEY SHARE < FOR SHARE < FOR NO KEY UPDATE < FOR UPDATE — finer modes reduce contention.

questions.prompt: Advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) differ from row/table locks in that they:

options.option_text: Are application-defined locks on arbitrary 64-bit keys, unrelated to data

questions.explanation: Advisory locks are cooperative semaphores keyed by app-defined numbers — useful for app-level mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: An index primarily helps by:

options.option_text: Reducing the number of rows the server must examine for matching queries

questions.explanation: Indexes map keys to row locations; selective predicates avoid full scans — at the cost of write/space overhead.

questions.prompt: A multicolumn B-tree index on (a, b) most directly supports:

options.option_text: Queries constraining a (leftmost columns), and (a,b) together
Queries on b alone equally well

questions.explanation: B-tree keys are ordered left-to-right; equality/range on leftmost prefixes use the index efficiently.

questions.prompt: A partial index WHERE status = 'open' is appropriate when:

options.option_text: Queries commonly filter status='open' and open rows are a small fraction

questions.explanation: Partial indexes cover only predicate-matching rows — smaller/faster when hot queries match the predicate.

questions.prompt: An index on lower(email) helps:
questions.explanation: Expression indexes index a function's result; the query must use the same expression to benefit.

questions.prompt: An index-only scan avoids visiting the table when:

options.option_text: All needed columns are in the index and the visibility map marks pages all-visible

questions.explanation: Index-only scans return index data directly, but MVCC requires the visibility map to confirm rows are visible to all.

questions.prompt: Which workload symptom does NOT fit 'add an index'?

options.option_text: ORDER BY sorts huge intermediate results
Frequent bulk INSERTs are getting slower
WHERE on an unindexed column does seq scans
JOIN keys produce nested-loop seq scans

questions.explanation: Indexes cost write overhead; heavy-insert workloads suffer more indexes. The other symptoms are classic index wins.

questions.prompt: The default and most general-purpose PostgreSQL index type is:

options.option_text: B-tree — handles equality and range ordering on sortable data

questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX defaults to B-tree, good for <, <=, =, >=, >, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL and ordered scans.

questions.prompt: GIN indexes are best suited for:

options.option_text: Composite values queried by membership — jsonb, arrays, tsvector

questions.explanation: GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes element→row postings, powering @>, ?, @@ searches.

questions.prompt: BRIN indexes work best when:

options.option_text: The table is huge and physical row order correlates with the indexed column (e.g. append-time timestamps)
Columns have few distinct values on small tables

questions.explanation: BRIN stores per-block-range min/max — tiny and fast when correlation exists, useless on uncorrelated data.

questions.prompt: GiST versus SP-GiST:

options.option_text: GiST is a balanced-tree framework for range/geometric semantics; SP-GiST is space-partitioned (quad/k-d/radix) for non-balanced partitions

questions.explanation: Both are extensible frameworks: GiST for overlapping-region types (ranges, geometry), SP-GiST for partitioned spaces.

questions.prompt: In EXPLAIN output, 'cost=0.00..183.34 rows=10000' the two numbers are:

options.option_text: Startup cost and total estimated cost in arbitrary planner units

questions.explanation: Costs are planner units (roughly page-fetches); the first is cost until first row output, second is total.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN ANALYZE differs from plain EXPLAIN in that it:

options.option_text: Actually executes the query and reports real timings/row counts alongside estimates

questions.explanation: ANALYZE runs the statement (DML affects data! — wrap in transaction), showing actual vs estimated rows per node.

questions.prompt: A 'Seq Scan' plan node means:

options.option_text: The whole table is read row-by-row — appropriate for unselective queries or small tables

questions.explanation: Sequential scan isn't inherently bad — when most rows match or the table is small, it beats index access.

questions.prompt: Bitmap Heap Scan + Bitmap Index Scan typically appears when:

options.option_text: An index finds many rows — the bitmap loses ordering but reads heap pages efficiently once

questions.explanation: For moderate selectivity, PostgreSQL collects TIDs into a bitmap then reads heap in physical order — between seq and index scan.

questions.prompt: Estimated rows=10 vs actual rows=500000 in EXPLAIN ANALYZE suggests:

options.option_text: Stale or missing statistics — run ANALYZE; the planner chose a plan for wrong cardinalities

questions.explanation: Plan quality depends on selectivity estimates from ANALYZE statistics; big skew → bad join/scan choices.

questions.prompt: ANALYZE collects what for the planner?

options.option_text: Column statistics — value distributions, common values, correlation — used for cardinality estimates

questions.explanation: ANALYZE samples each table building pg_statistic entries; autovacuum also auto-analyzes changed tables.

questions.prompt: default_statistics_target / column statistics targets control:

options.option_text: Sample size and histogram granularity — higher targets estimate skewed distributions better at ANALYZE cost

questions.explanation: Raising the target improves plan quality on skewed data but slows ANALYZE and planner work.

questions.prompt: Correlated columns (e.g. city within state) fool the planner because:

options.option_text: Per-column statistics assume independence — CREATE STATISTICS captures the dependency

questions.explanation: Extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS: ndistinct, dependencies, mcv) fix multi-column correlation misestimates.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, 'user' and 'group' are both:

options.option_text: Roles — a user is a role with LOGIN; a group is a role containing members

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL unifies users/groups as roles; LOGIN attribute permits connections, membership gives inherited rights.

questions.prompt: Role attributes like CREATEDB and CREATEROLE are:

options.option_text: Capabilities assigned to roles, separate from object privileges

questions.explanation: Attributes (LOGIN, SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS) are role flags granted at CREATE/ALTER ROLE.

questions.prompt: With INHERIT (default), a member role:

options.option_text: Automatically has the privileges of roles it belongs to
Must SET ROLE to gain them

questions.explanation: INHERIT makes membership rights immediate; NOINHERIT requires explicit SET ROLE to assume the group role.

questions.prompt: GRANT SELECT ON t TO analyst permits:

options.option_text: The analyst role to read table t

questions.explanation: Object privileges are per-object-type action rights; WITH GRANT OPTION would additionally allow re-granting.

questions.prompt: GRANT ... WITH GRANT OPTION means the grantee:

options.option_text: May grant the same privilege to other roles

questions.explanation: Grant option delegates administration of that privilege; REVOKE cascades through dependent grants.

questions.prompt: Column-level privileges (GRANT SELECT (a, b) ON t) allow:

options.option_text: Reading only listed columns — unlisted columns error on access

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports per-column SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/REFERENCES grants for fine-grained access.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY without any policy means:

options.option_text: Default-deny — non-owner roles see no rows

questions.explanation: With RLS enabled and no policy, a default-deny applies; the owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE is set.

questions.prompt: A policy's USING clause versus WITH CHECK clause:

options.option_text: USING filters rows visible to queries; WITH CHECK validates rows being written

questions.explanation: USING(expression) determines existing-row visibility; WITH CHECK(expression) constrains new/modified row values.

questions.prompt: Permissive versus restrictive policies combine:

options.option_text: Only one policy per table is allowed
Multiple permissive policies OR together; restrictive policies AND together

questions.explanation: Rows must pass at least one permissive AND all restrictive policies — mixing gives AND-of-restrictive with OR-of-permissive.

questions.prompt: Who bypasses row security by default?

options.option_text: Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS, and the table owner (unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY)

questions.explanation: Owner bypass needs ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY to close; superusers/BYPASSRLS always bypass.

questions.prompt: CREATE FUNCTION f(int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql AS 'SELECT $1 * 2' defines:

options.option_text: A SQL-language function doubling its argument

questions.explanation: SQL functions evaluate expressions/queries; $1 is the first argument.

questions.prompt: IMMUTABLE / STABLE / VOLATILE function categories describe:

options.option_text: Whether results depend only on inputs — guiding planner optimization and index use

questions.explanation: IMMUTABLE = same input→same output forever (index-safe); STABLE = constant within a statement; VOLATILE = anything.

questions.prompt: Why must an indexed expression like lower(email) only use IMMUTABLE functions?

options.option_text: It is a syntax requirement only
Index entries must never change for a given row

questions.explanation: If the expression could change without a row update, index entries would lie — PostgreSQL enforces immutability.

questions.prompt: RETURNS SETOF int and RETURNS TABLE(id int, name text) both mean:

options.option_text: The function returns a set of rows, usable in FROM

questions.explanation: Set-returning functions produce rows; TABLE(...) names the output columns.

questions.prompt: SECURITY DEFINER on a function means:

options.option_text: It executes with the privileges of its owner, not the caller

questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER functions run as owner — powerful for controlled access but dangerous if they take unvalidated input.

questions.prompt: A PL/pgSQL function body is structured as:
questions.explanation: PL/pgSQL is block-structured: optional label, DECLARE section, BEGIN/END body — blocks nest.

questions.prompt: Inside PL/pgSQL, assignment uses:
questions.explanation: := is the classic assignment; plain = is also accepted for assignment.

questions.prompt: FOUND in PL/pgSQL reports:

options.option_text: Whether the last SQL statement affected/returned rows

questions.explanation: The boolean FOUND is set after SELECT INTO, DML, FOR loops etc. — the idiom for 'did my statement do anything'.

questions.prompt: EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN ... in a BEGIN block:

options.option_text: Catches that error and continues after the block — like try/catch with subtransaction semantics

questions.explanation: EXCEPTION handlers trap matching SQLSTATE conditions; the failed substatement rolls back to the block start.

questions.prompt: %TYPE and %ROWTYPE in declarations:

options.option_text: Anchor a variable's type to a column or row structure, surviving schema changes

questions.explanation: DECLARE v emp.name%TYPE pins v to that column's type; %ROWTYPE captures whole-row structure.

questions.prompt: CREATE PROCEDURE differs from CREATE FUNCTION mainly because procedures:

options.option_text: Are invoked with CALL, can manage transactions (COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside), and return no value

questions.explanation: Procedures (PG 11+) run via CALL and may perform transaction control — functions cannot.

questions.prompt: To run a procedure p(5):
questions.explanation: CALL invokes procedures; SELECT invokes functions.

questions.prompt: A BEFORE INSERT row trigger function returning NULL means:

options.option_text: The insert for that row is skipped

questions.explanation: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger cancels the operation for that row; returning NEW proceeds.

questions.prompt: Inside a row-level trigger, NEW and OLD refer to:

options.option_text: The new and old row versions (NEW on INSERT/UPDATE, OLD on UPDATE/DELETE)

questions.explanation: Trigger functions get NEW (proposed row) and/or OLD (existing row) depending on TG_OP.

questions.prompt: FOR EACH ROW versus FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers:

options.option_text: Row triggers fire once per affected row; statement triggers once per statement
ROW triggers are faster on bulk ops

questions.explanation: Granularity choice: per-row logic (audit columns, validation) vs once-per-statement summary work.

questions.prompt: INSTEAD OF triggers exist primarily for:

options.option_text: Making non-updatable views writable — the trigger defines what the DML does

questions.explanation: INSTEAD OF triggers intercept view DML; the function performs the real base-table operations.

questions.prompt: The classic audit-trail pattern (BEFORE UPDATE, set NEW.updated_at = now()) works because:

options.option_text: A BEFORE trigger can modify NEW before it is written
AFTER triggers can modify stored rows

questions.explanation: BEFORE row triggers may rewrite fields of NEW — the canonical way to stamp audit columns.

questions.prompt: shared_buffers controls:

options.option_text: How much memory PostgreSQL dedicates to its shared page cache

questions.explanation: shared_buffers is the main in-memory data cache; too small starves caching, too big wastes OS cache.

questions.prompt: work_mem is consumed:

options.option_text: Per sort/hash operation — a single query may use several times work_mem across nodes

questions.explanation: work_mem bounds each sort/hash node; complex plans multiply it — over-aggressive values cause memory pressure.

questions.prompt: ALTER SYSTEM SET x = y writes to:

options.option_text: postgresql.auto.conf, applied on reload/restart per the parameter's context

questions.explanation: ALTER SYSTEM persists to postgresql.auto.conf (included by postgresql.conf); some params need restart or reload.

questions.prompt: The main reason PostgreSQL needs VACUUM is:

options.option_text: To reclaim space from dead row versions left by MVCC updates/deletes

questions.explanation: MVCC retains dead tuples until VACUUM marks their space reusable — without it, tables bloat unboundedly.

questions.prompt: Standard VACUUM versus VACUUM FULL:

options.option_text: VACUUM frees space for reuse in-place and allows concurrent access; FULL rewrites the table compacted, holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE

questions.explanation: Regular VACUUM is online (table stays usable); FULL compacts to minimum size but blocks all access.

questions.prompt: Autovacuum is triggered primarily by:

options.option_text: The number of dead/updated tuples crossing per-table thresholds

questions.explanation: The autovacuum daemon launches workers when dead-tuple estimates exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + scale_factor×rows.

questions.prompt: Transaction ID wraparound protection requires vacuuming because:

options.option_text: The 32-bit XID space recycles — unfrozen old tuples could become 'invisible' as future transactions misread them

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses ~4B XIDs; VACUUM FREEZE marks old tuples permanently visible before wraparound would corrupt visibility.

questions.prompt: pg_dump produces:

options.option_text: A binary image of the data directory
A logical SQL-level backup of one database, consistent at dump time

questions.explanation: pg_dump emits SQL (or custom-format) for one DB; pg_dumpall covers the whole cluster including roles.

questions.prompt: To back up cluster-global objects like roles and tablespaces, use:
questions.explanation: pg_dump doesn't capture roles/tablespaces — pg_dumpall dumps them plus every database.

questions.prompt: Continuous archiving (WAL archiving + base backup) uniquely enables:

options.option_text: Point-in-time recovery to any moment between backups

questions.explanation: Replaying archived WAL atop a base backup restores to an arbitrary timestamp — pg_dump cannot do this.

questions.prompt: The Write-Ahead Log exists primarily to:

options.option_text: Guarantee durability — changes are logged to stable storage before data pages, enabling crash recovery

questions.explanation: WAL records changes; after a crash, recovery replays WAL to reach a consistent state — the 'log first' rule.

questions.prompt: A checkpoint in PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Flushes dirty data pages so recovery need only replay WAL after the checkpoint

questions.explanation: Checkpoints bound crash-recovery work: pages before the checkpoint are guaranteed on disk, enabling WAL recycling.

questions.prompt: Streaming (physical) replication ships:

options.option_text: WAL records — a byte-level copy of the cluster to a standby

questions.explanation: Physical replication streams WAL: the standby replays to stay byte-identical — whole-cluster, read-only replica.

questions.prompt: Logical replication differs in that it:

options.option_text: Replicates row-level changes of selected tables via publication/subscription

questions.explanation: Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes per publication — flexible subsets, cross-version possible.

questions.prompt: A replication slot guarantees:

options.option_text: The primary retains WAL needed by the subscriber/standby — preventing premature recycling

questions.explanation: Slots pin WAL on the primary; an abandoned slot can fill disk — a classic operational hazard.

questions.prompt: pg_stat_activity shows:

options.option_text: One row per server process — current query, state, wait info

questions.explanation: pg_stat_activity is the live 'who is doing what' view for diagnosing blocks and long queries.

questions.prompt: pg_stat_user_tables tracks per-table counters including:
questions.explanation: Cumulative stats views expose scan counts and dead tuples — the first stop for bloat/index-usage checks.

questions.prompt: USING (dept_id) versus ON a.dept_id = b.dept_id differ because:

options.option_text: USING merges the matched columns into one output column

questions.explanation: USING produces a single coalesced output column per join key; ON keeps both sides' columns.

questions.prompt: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE ...) tests:

options.option_text: Whether the subquery returns at least one row — content irrelevant
That the subquery returns exactly one row

questions.explanation: EXISTS is true if the subquery yields any row; correlated EXISTS links it to the outer row.

questions.prompt: SELECT t.* FROM t selects:

options.option_text: All columns of the aliased table t only
All columns of every table in FROM

questions.explanation: alias.* scopes the star to one FROM item — useful in joins to grab one side's columns.

questions.prompt: VALUES (1,'a'),(2,'b') used in FROM produces:
questions.explanation: VALUES lists construct constant tables usable anywhere a table is — joins, inserts, CTEs.

questions.prompt: CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy') creates:

options.option_text: A static ordered set of labels — values compare by declaration order

questions.explanation: Enum labels are fixed at type creation; ordering is the declaration order and storage is compact.

questions.prompt: Adding a value to an existing enum type uses:

options.option_text: ALTER TYPE mood ADD VALUE 'calm' (with ordering options BEFORE/AFTER)

questions.explanation: ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE appends (or positions) a new label; new values can't be used in the same transaction under older versions.

questions.prompt: The uuid type is preferred over text for identifiers because it:

options.option_text: Stores 16 bytes compactly and validates format

questions.explanation: uuid is a dedicated 128-bit type with literal validation; generation needs functions like gen_random_uuid().

questions.prompt: inet / cidr types represent:

options.option_text: IPv4/IPv6 host addresses and networks with containment operators

questions.explanation: Network types support >>, <<= containment and other operators for subnet logic.

questions.prompt: A sequence object (nextval('seq')):

options.option_text: Is tied to one column only
Produces monotonically increasing numbers shareable across tables

questions.explanation: Sequences are standalone counter objects; nextval is not transactional — rolled-back values leave gaps.

questions.prompt: Why can identity/serial columns have gaps even without deletes?

options.option_text: nextval increments are not rolled back when a transaction aborts

questions.explanation: Sequence increments are outside MVCC rollback — aborted inserts consume values permanently, so gaps are normal.

questions.prompt: pg_hba.conf controls:

options.option_text: Which hosts/users/databases may connect and by what authentication method

questions.explanation: Host-based authentication rules are matched top-down; first match wins — changes need a reload.

questions.prompt: The recommended password authentication method in modern PostgreSQL is:
questions.explanation: SCRAM-SHA-256 is the challenge-response standard; md5 is legacy, trust skips auth entirely.

questions.prompt: A 'serialization failure' error (SQLSTATE 40001) means:

options.option_text: The transaction's execution could not be proven serializable — retry it

questions.explanation: Serializable mode aborts transactions forming dangerous rw-antidependency cycles; clients must be ready to retry.

questions.prompt: Serializable isolation is stronger than Repeatable Read because it also prevents:

options.option_text: Phantom rows only (RR already allows them)
Serialization anomalies — executions whose result couldn't occur in any serial order

questions.explanation: Serializable adds anomaly detection atop the RR snapshot; the write-skew pattern is the classic anomaly it blocks.

questions.prompt: 'Table bloat' in PostgreSQL refers to:

options.option_text: Accumulation of dead row versions making tables/indexes larger and slower than the live data requires

questions.explanation: Every UPDATE/DELETE leaves dead tuples; if VACUUM can't keep pace they inflate scans — the bloat/vacuum relationship.

questions.prompt: Why does COUNT(*) stay relatively expensive in PostgreSQL on huge tables?

options.option_text: MVCC visibility must be checked per row version — there is no cheap exact counter

questions.explanation: Without a single row store, each tuple's visibility must be verified; index-only scans help when the visibility map is hot.

questions.prompt: max_connections sets:

options.option_text: The ceiling on simultaneous client connections to the server

questions.explanation: Beyond max_connections, new connections are refused; pooling (e.g. PgBouncer) manages excess clients.

questions.prompt: The visibility map supports:

options.option_text: Index-only scans — pages marked all-visible need no heap fetch to confirm row visibility

questions.explanation: VACUUM marks all-visible pages in the VM; index-only scans consult it before skipping heap access.

questions.prompt: pg_dump custom format (-Fc) versus plain SQL:

options.option_text: Compressed archive restorable selectively via pg_restore

questions.explanation: Custom/directory formats compress and allow selective restore/reorder; plain SQL needs psql replay in full.

questions.prompt: A limitation of filesystem-level backup is:

options.option_text: It needs the whole data directory snapshotted atomically with the server stopped or properly frozen

questions.explanation: Copying a live data dir without freeze/snapshot yields torn files; PITR or offline copies are the safe routes.

questions.prompt: A synchronous streaming replica differs from asynchronous because:

options.option_text: synchronous_commit waits for standby confirmation before acknowledging commit — trading latency for lower RPO

questions.explanation: sync replication confirms WAL reached the standby; async can lose recent commits on failover.
