questions.prompt: pg_stat_statements (extension) provides:

options.option_text: Aggregated per-query statistics — calls, total time, rows — for finding expensive query patterns

questions.explanation: It fingerprints normalized queries and accumulates timing/count stats — the standard top-query tool.

questions.prompt: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT requires which to work deterministically?

options.option_text: A matching unique index or constraint on the conflict target columns

questions.explanation: The conflict target must map to a unique index/constraint for the inference of which violation occurred.

questions.prompt: An EXCLUSION constraint (e.g. no overlapping booking ranges) enforces:

options.option_text: Row-pairwise operator checks — no two rows may satisfy the operators on the same keys

questions.explanation: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, span WITH &&) forbids overlapping ranges — declarative no-double-booking.

questions.prompt: CUBE(a, b) produces grouping sets:
questions.explanation: CUBE enumerates the power set of its columns — cross-tab style multi-dimensional aggregation.

questions.prompt: ORDER BY can reference columns not in the select list:

options.option_text: Only when no DISTINCT or set operation is present

questions.explanation: With DISTINCT/UNION the sort keys must appear in the output so the result is well-defined.

questions.prompt: EXCEPT NULL-handling: for row comparisons in set operations, NULLs are treated as:

options.option_text: Equal to one another — a NULL row matches a NULL row

questions.explanation: Set operations use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM semantics — NULLs count as equal for dedup/intersect/except.

questions.prompt: ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY x) divides rows into:

options.option_text: Four buckets as evenly as possible, numbered 1-4

questions.explanation: ntile buckets the ordered rows into n near-equal groups — the ranking-family 'quantile' function.

questions.prompt: WITH regional AS (SELECT ...) SELECT * FROM regional — the CTE name scope is:

options.option_text: Only the statement that defines it

questions.explanation: CTE names live for the duration of one query — like an inline temporary view.

questions.prompt: BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 10 AND 5:

options.option_text: Is valid — swaps bounds so 5..10 is tested

questions.explanation: SYMMETRIC removes the requirement that the lower bound be written first.

questions.prompt: coalesce(NULL, NULL, 3) and greatest(1, NULL, 5) return respectively:
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument; GREATEST and LEAST ignore NULL inputs in PostgreSQL, picking 5 here.

questions.prompt: x > ALL(SELECT ...) is true when:

options.option_text: x exceeds every row the subquery returns (or the subquery is empty)
x exceeds at least one row

questions.explanation: ALL requires the comparison hold against every result row — vacuously true on empty sets (a subtle trap).

questions.prompt: x IN (subquery) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: IN expands to = ANY — true when x equals any returned row; the empty-set case yields false.

questions.prompt: A self-join (emp e JOIN emp m ON e.mgr_id = m.id) is used for:

options.option_text: Relating rows of a table to other rows of the same table — like employees to managers

questions.explanation: Self-joins need aliases to distinguish the two roles of the same relation.

questions.prompt: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW versus RANGE over the same ORDER BY:

options.option_text: ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE includes all peers with equal sort-key values
ROWS is illegal without PARTITION BY

questions.explanation: RANGE's frame spans value-peers; ROWS's frame counts row positions — peers matter for ties.

questions.prompt: first_value(x) OVER w and last_value(x) OVER w on a full-partition frame give:

options.option_text: The first and last row's x in window order — last_value needs UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to see the partition end

questions.explanation: With the default frame ending at CURRENT ROW, last_value returns the current row — the classic frame trap.

questions.prompt: WITH ... AS NOT MATERIALIZED requests:

options.option_text: Inlining the CTE into the query so the planner can optimize it jointly

questions.explanation: NOT MATERIALIZED hints the planner to fold the subquery in — overriding the multi-reference materialization default.

questions.prompt: SELECT 'a' UNION SELECT 'b' ORDER BY 1 sorts by:

options.option_text: The output column — set-operation results sort on the combined column
An error — ORDER BY needs table columns

questions.explanation: After a set op, ORDER BY refers to result columns (name or position), not source columns.

questions.prompt: An INNER JOIN ON true (or 1=1) behaves as:

options.option_text: A cross join — every row pairs with every row

questions.explanation: A tautological join condition degenerates to a Cartesian product.

questions.prompt: SELECT DISTINCT ON is:

options.option_text: A PostgreSQL extension — not standard SQL

questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL-specific syntax providing a concise per-group first-row idiom.

questions.prompt: OFFSET without LIMIT in PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Is legal — it skips N rows and returns the rest

questions.explanation: OFFSET alone is permitted; rows after the skipped prefix are returned in arbitrary order without ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: START TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE, READ ONLY:

options.option_text: Begins a transaction with fixed mode flags — useful for consistent report snapshots

questions.explanation: Transaction modes (isolation, read-write/read-only, deferrable) are set at BEGIN/START or per-statement.

questions.prompt: A READ ONLY DEFERRABLE serializable transaction is the documented pattern for:

options.option_text: Long-running consistent reports that avoid blocking and serialization aborts

questions.explanation: Deferrable read-only serializable transactions wait for a 'safe' snapshot — ideal for consistent exports.

questions.prompt: FOR UPDATE ... NOWAIT versus FOR UPDATE ... SKIP LOCKED:

options.option_text: NOWAIT errors immediately if a row is locked; SKIP LOCKED silently omits locked rows

questions.explanation: The two options serve different patterns: fail-fast vs work-queue-style 'grab free rows'.

questions.prompt: A covering index (INCLUDE (col)) lets index-only scans return:

options.option_text: The included columns without adding them to the index's sort/search keys

questions.explanation: INCLUDE stores extra payload columns in index entries — covering queries without widening the key.

questions.prompt: Hash indexes in modern PostgreSQL:

options.option_text: Are WAL-logged and useful for equality on large values, but B-tree usually suffices

questions.explanation: Hash indexes are crash-safe since v10 but narrow in utility (equality only); B-tree dominates practice.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) adds:

options.option_text: Buffer hit/read counts per node — revealing actual I/O vs cache hits

questions.explanation: BUFFERS instruments shared/local hits+reads, the key signal for I/O-bound plan nodes.

questions.prompt: SET search_path = '$user', public means unqualified names resolve:

options.option_text: First in a schema named after the user (if it exists), then public

questions.explanation: $user is the current user's namesake schema slot; pg_catalog is always searched implicitly first unless listed.

questions.prompt: REVOKE ... CASCADE versus RESTRICT:

options.option_text: CASCADE revokes dependent grants made via grant option; RESTRICT fails if any exist

questions.explanation: When a grantee re-granted via grant option, CASCADE removes the chain; RESTRICT protects against surprise revocation.

questions.prompt: Default privileges (ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES) exist to:

options.option_text: Auto-grant privileges on objects a role creates in future — avoiding per-object GRANTs

questions.explanation: Default privileges apply at object creation time — e.g. app tables auto-readable by a reporting role.

questions.prompt: PERFORM query in PL/pgSQL:

options.option_text: Executes a SELECT discarding results — for side effects without SELECT INTO

questions.explanation: PERFORM runs a query whose result is dropped — the PL/pgSQL way to call SELECT for effect.

questions.prompt: GET DIAGNOSTICS row_count = ROW_COUNT after DML in PL/pgSQL gives:

options.option_text: The number of rows the last statement processed

questions.explanation: GET DIAGNOSTICS retrieves statement metadata; FOUND is the simpler boolean version.

questions.prompt: A statement-level trigger cannot see NEW/OLD because:

options.option_text: NEW/OLD are per-row objects — statement granularity has no single row; use transition tables instead

questions.explanation: For statement triggers needing row access, REFERENCING NEW TABLE/OLD TABLE exposes transition relations.

questions.prompt: Function overloading in PostgreSQL permits:

options.option_text: Multiple functions sharing a name if their argument type lists differ

questions.explanation: Functions are identified by name+arg types; return type alone cannot disambiguate.

questions.prompt: ANALYZE inside autovacuum's duties:

options.option_text: Refreshes planner statistics when enough rows changed — separate from dead-tuple cleanup

questions.explanation: The daemon schedules both vacuum (dead tuples) and analyze (stats) per change thresholds.

questions.prompt: WAL archiving (archive_mode) means:

options.option_text: Completed WAL segments are copied to safe storage for PITR/replication

questions.explanation: archive_command copies each finished segment — the foundation of continuous archiving.

questions.prompt: Logical replication publications select:

options.option_text: Which tables' row changes are offered to subscribers

questions.explanation: CREATE PUBLICATION FOR TABLE lists what to replicate; subscriptions pull the decoded changes.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE t2 (LIKE t1 INCLUDING ALL) creates:

options.option_text: A new empty table copying t1's columns plus all defaults, constraints, and indexes

questions.explanation: LIKE clones structure; INCLUDING options choose which features (indexes, defaults, constraints) to carry.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE AS (CTAS) versus CREATE VIEW:

options.option_text: CTAS stores a physical snapshot at creation; a view re-evaluates its query each use

questions.explanation: CTAS materializes once — like a one-time materialized view; the base data changes are never reflected.

questions.prompt: NOT VALID on ADD CONSTRAINT means:

options.option_text: New rows are checked but existing rows are trusted — the scan/lock is deferred to VALIDATE CONSTRAINT

questions.explanation: NOT VALID + later VALIDATE minimizes locking during rollout of constraints on big populated tables.

questions.prompt: Attaching an existing table as a partition uses:

options.option_text: ALTER TABLE parent ATTACH PARTITION child FOR VALUES ...

questions.explanation: ATTACH PARTITION moves a table under the partitioned parent — bulk-loading pattern: load, then attach.

questions.prompt: Concatenating text with NULL ('a' || NULL) yields:
questions.explanation: String concatenation propagates NULL — use concat() or COALESCE for null-safe concatenation.

questions.prompt: timestamp without time zone versus timestamptz semantics:

options.option_text: timestamp stores a wall-clock with no zone awareness; timestamptz an absolute instant

questions.explanation: timestamp is a calendar/clock reading with no instant meaning; timestamptz normalizes input to UTC.

questions.prompt: jsonb_each(doc) returns:

options.option_text: A set of (key text, value jsonb) rows — expanding the top-level object

questions.explanation: jsonb_each explodes an object's top-level pairs — the extraction tool for unknown key sets.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL never lets readers block writers under MVCC. Explain how multiversioning achieves this, what a 'snapshot' means concretely for a transaction, and what maintenance duty this design creates.
questions.reference_answer: Each UPDATE/DELETE writes a new tuple version while old versions persist for snapshots that may still see them. A transaction's snapshot fixes which commits are visible; readers traverse the version chain instead of locking. The cost is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim — bloat and the visibility-map/ID-wraparound machinery exist because of this trade.

rubrics.criteria: Believes MVCC is just row locking or confuses it with replication
Knows reads don't block writes but cannot explain versions or maintenance
Explains snapshots and dead tuples; minor imprecision on wraparound or visibility map
Explains MVCC visibility rules, version churn and vacuum's role with correct detail

questions.explanation: MVCC fundamentals — Ch. 13 and the vacuum chapter are the two sides of this design.

questions.prompt: A colleague says 'Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL prevents every anomaly, so we never need Serializable.' Evaluate this claim precisely: which anomalies each level blocks, what a serialization anomaly looks like (use write skew), and what error handling Serializable requires.
questions.reference_answer: Repeatable Read gives a transaction-long snapshot — no dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads — but admits serialization anomalies: results impossible under any serial order. Write skew example: two on-call rules where each transaction reads a count > 0 then removes itself, leaving zero — both commit under RR. Serializable (SSI) detects such rw-antidependency structures and aborts one party; applications must catch SQLSTATE 40001 and retry.

rubrics.criteria: Agrees with the claim or confuses isolation levels
Knows Serializable is 'stronger' but cannot name what it prevents that RR allows
Correct anomaly taxonomy and knows serialization failures exist; scenario or retry detail loose
Correctly distinguishes RR from Serializable, gives a sound write-skew scenario, and states the retry contract

questions.explanation: Isolation-level precision — Table 13.1 of the manual lists exactly which phenomena each level allows.

questions.prompt: You must index: (a) equality+range lookups on an order_date column, (b) jsonb containment queries, (c) a 500M-row append-only events table queried by event_ts, physically clustered by time, (d) an array 'tags' membership check. Choose index types and justify each choice including its tradeoffs.
questions.reference_answer: B-tree for (a) — ordered comparisons on sortable data. GIN for (b) and (d) — inverted posting lists for containment of elements/keys. BRIN for (c) — block-range summaries exploit physical ordering, tiny index on huge correlated data; it fails on uncorrelated data. Tradeoffs: GIN write cost, BRIN only for correlated data, B-tree size but general utility.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests B-tree for everything or invents index types
Names some index types but not matched to workloads
Correct types with thin justification, or one swap defended plausibly
Correct type per workload with the physical reasoning for each

questions.explanation: Index-type selection is about data shape and query operators, not 'indexes make it faster'.

questions.prompt: A dashboard query is slow. Walk through how you would use EXPLAIN ANALYZE output (cost vs actual rows, scan types, buffers, loops) to diagnose it, and what stale statistics have to do with plan quality.
questions.reference_answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query showing per-node estimated vs actual rows, real time, and (BUFFERS) I/O. Big estimate/actual divergence indicates stale or inadequate statistics — ANALYZE (and statistics targets/extended stats) fixes planner input. Scan-type reasoning: seq scan on an unselective predicate is fine; nested loops with huge inner counts signal bad cardinality estimates; loops > 1 multiply child costs.

rubrics.criteria: No coherent diagnostic method
Knows EXPLAIN exists; cannot interpret cost/rows or scan choices
Reads plans correctly; misses the statistics/estimate connection or buffers detail
Correct diagnosis workflow: estimate vs actual, buffers, loop multipliers, statistics link

questions.explanation: Plan literacy is the core performance skill: estimates drive choices, ANALYZE feeds estimates.

questions.prompt: When should a PostgreSQL design use jsonb columns instead of normalized relational columns — and when must it not? Cover storage/indexing differences, query ergonomics, integrity guarantees and a concrete scenario for each choice.
questions.reference_answer: jsonb fits genuinely schemaless/sparse/evolving attributes and document-shaped payloads — GIN indexes support @>, ?, ?|. It forfeits column-level types, constraints, foreign keys and statistics; predicates need operators clients must know. Normalized columns fit structured, queried, constrained data — the default. Anti-pattern: burying relational keys inside jsonb blobs to avoid schema work.

rubrics.criteria: Recommends jsonb everywhere or nowhere categorically
Knows jsonb exists but argues by convenience not structure
Correct json vs jsonb + indexing facts; weaker judgment on when to choose each
Balanced criteria with correct jsonb mechanics and integrity analysis plus valid scenarios

questions.explanation: jsonb is a complement to the relational model, not a schema-free shortcut.

questions.prompt: Design a partitioning strategy for a multi-billion-row events table queried mostly by recent time windows, with cheap retention (drop old months). Cover partition method/key, pruning, the retention operation, unique-constraint implications and operational gotchas.
questions.reference_answer: PARTITION BY RANGE (event_ts) monthly; queries with event_ts predicates prune to few partitions. Retention = DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY or DROP on old monthly partitions — O(1) vs DELETE+VACUUM. Unique constraints must include the partition key — a global PK on id alone is impossible without event_ts. Gotchas: no pruning if the key isn't in WHERE, default partition traps, ATTACH for bulk loads, per-partition indexes.

rubrics.criteria: Proposes DELETE-based retention or non-existent partition syntax
Knows partitioning exists; fuzzy on method or benefits
Correct partition choice and retention; misses the key-in-unique-constraint or pruning caveat
Complete correct design with pruning, retention mechanics, PK constraint and pitfalls

questions.explanation: Partitioning is a data-lifecycle feature — pruning and cheap detach are the wins.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS stores all tenants' rows in shared tables. Compare three isolation designs: separate databases, schema-per-tenant, and shared tables + row-level security. Then specify the RLS policy needed (including FORCE and the migration risk) for tenant isolation.
questions.reference_answer: Separate DBs = strongest isolation, worst ops/schema proliferation. Schema-per-tenant = middle. Shared+RLS = simplest ops; CREATE POLICY tenant_iso ON t USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int) per table, ENABLE + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY so owners don't bypass. Risks: BYPASSRLS/superuser leaks, forgetting FORCE, leakproof-function ordering, policy expression cost on every query.

rubrics.criteria: Claims GRANT alone enforces tenant isolation
Mentions RLS without usable mechanics
Correct policy core; misses FORCE or one alternative model
Compares the three models and writes a correct policy incl. FORCE + bypass caveats

questions.explanation: RLS is the standard shared-schema tenancy tool — but it is opt-in and easily misconfigured.

questions.prompt: An autovacuum is falling behind on a high-churn table: dead tuples grow faster than workers reclaim them. Explain the symptoms (bloat, plan drift), the tuning knobs available, and why VACUUM FULL is not the routine answer.
questions.reference_answer: Symptoms: table/index bloat, slower scans, wasted space, wraparound risk if very old. Knobs: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor/cost_limit/vacuum_cost_delay per-table via storage parameters, more workers. FULL rewrites with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — blocks all access; used for reclamation, not steady-state. The real fix is tuning frequency/aggressiveness and HOT-update-friendly fillfactor.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests routine VACUUM FULL or disabling autovacuum
Knows vacuum exists; cannot diagnose or tune
Correct on autovacuum role; thin on specific parameters or locking
Correct symptoms, per-table autovacuum tuning and FULL's lock semantics

questions.explanation: Autovacuum tuning is workload-shaped — per-table storage parameters are the instrument.

questions.prompt: Design a backup strategy for a 500GB OLTP database requiring RPO ~ 0 and recovery to any minute in the last 30 days. Explain the components (base backup, WAL archive, testing) and why pg_dump alone cannot satisfy the requirements.
questions.reference_answer: Continuous archiving: scheduled base backups (pg_basebackup or tool) + WAL archive via archive_command to durable storage → PITR to any timestamp. pg_dump is a logical snapshot — consistent but point-in-time only as of dump start, no incremental replay; restores are full and slow. Recovery testing and monitoring the archive are mandatory; a backup that was never restored is a hope not a strategy.

rubrics.criteria: No viable design
Knows backups exist; proposes nightly pg_dump for RPO 0
PITR architecture correct; misses testing or pg_dump limitation nuance
Correct PITR architecture with base backup+WAL, RPO reasoning and restore-testing

questions.explanation: PITR = base backup + continuous WAL; dumps are for logical portability, not tight RPO.

questions.prompt: Choose between streaming (physical) and logical replication for these needs and justify: (a) a hot standby for failover, (b) replicating two tables to a reporting database on a different major version, (c) minimal-lag read scaling. Include the replication-slot disk-growth hazard.
questions.reference_answer: Physical streaming for (a) and (c) — byte-identical standby, WAL streaming, synchronous option for failover; read-only queries serve reporting/load. Logical for (b) — row changes per publication cross versions and subset tables. Slots pin WAL on the primary; a dead subscriber grows pg_wal until disk-full — monitor slot lag.

rubrics.criteria: Confuses replication with backup or partitioning
Names replication types without clear criteria
Correct basic split physical vs logical; light on justifications or slots
Correct matching with reasons and the slot hazard

questions.explanation: Physical = whole-cluster byte copy; logical = selective row changes — different tools.

questions.prompt: Compare expressing a multi-step aggregation as nested subqueries versus WITH clauses. When does the CTE version perform differently (materialization) and when is it merely clearer? Give an example where materialization semantics matter.
questions.reference_answer: Pre-v12 CTEs were optimization fences always materialized; v12+ inlines singly-referenced non-recursive CTEs like views. MATERIALIZED forces one computation — valuable when an expensive result is referenced twice; NOT MATERIALIZED enables pushdown. Readability: named stages beat nested subqueries for pipelines; performance is now equivalent in the single-reference case.

rubrics.criteria: No distinction between subquery and CTE
Thinks CTEs are always faster or always slower
Knows CTEs inline now; vague on MATERIALIZED use-cases
Correct post-v12 semantics, when materialization helps/hurts, and readability argument

questions.explanation: CTE performance changed in v12 — the 'always materialized' folklore is outdated.

questions.prompt: Explain why SELECT dept, name, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp cannot be filtered by WHERE r = 1 — and the two correct ways to get 'top earner per dept' (window subquery vs DISTINCT ON). Compare them.
questions.reference_answer: Window functions evaluate after WHERE over the FROM/WHERE result — the rank doesn't exist yet at filtering time. Solution A: wrap the ranked query in a subquery and filter outside (ties kept with rank()). Solution B: PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON (dept) with ORDER BY dept, salary DESC — shorter, single row per group (no tie support without care). DISTINCT ON is PG-specific; the subquery is portable.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests putting the window call in WHERE or HAVING
Knows the error exists; cannot explain why
Explains WHERE limitation and one valid solution
Correct evaluation-order explanation and both solutions with the tie/portability comparison

questions.explanation: Logical evaluation order explains most 'why can't I' SQL errors — learn the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Two services update bank accounts and intermittently deadlock. Explain how the deadlock forms under MVCC (a row-lock ordering problem, not a read problem), what PostgreSQL does about it, and the design fixes (consistent ordering, NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED, shorter transactions).
questions.reference_answer: Tx1 locks row A then requests B while Tx2 holds B requesting A — a cycle. Readers/writers don't block under MVCC, but row write locks do; deadlock_timeout detection aborts one cycle member. Fixes: lock rows in a canonical order (e.g. by id), keep critical sections short, FOR UPDATE NOWAIT to fail fast or SKIP LOCKED for queue semantics, retry the aborted transaction.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests disabling deadlock detection or serializing all access
Blames reads/isolation level rather than lock ordering
Correct deadlock model; fixes generic
Accurate cycle explanation, detection semantics and ≥2 sound fixes

questions.explanation: Deadlocks are lock-ordering bugs; retries are part of the contract, not an accident.

questions.prompt: Compare serial, GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY and a stored generated column for an 'order_number' that must be sequential and for a 'line_total' computed from qty*price. Which mechanism fits each and what are the write-path rules?
questions.reference_answer: serial = sequence+default (overridable, gaps on rollback); IDENTITY ALWAYS = standard, system-controlled sequence, user values rejected unless OVERRIDING; GENERATED column = deterministic expression of same-row columns, no writes allowed at all. Sequential order_number → identity/serial; line_total → generated column since it derives from other columns.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests triggers for line_total or computed PKs
Conflates the three mechanisms
Distinguishes generated vs sequence; fuzzy on ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT
Correct mechanism per field with the write rules for each

questions.explanation: Sequences answer 'give me a number'; generated columns answer 'derive this value'.

questions.prompt: A finance dashboard aggregates yesterday's 50M rows in 8 seconds; management wants 5-minute freshness for an ops view and daily freshness for the finance view. Choose view vs materialized view per case and justify refresh strategy and staleness.
questions.reference_answer: Finance (daily): materialized view refreshed nightly/CONCURRENTLY — pays staleness for instant reads. Ops (5-min): a materialized view with 5-minute REFRESH CONCURRENTLY (needs unique index) or a plain view if the query is cheap — at 8s per refresh on 50M rows the matview is viable; a plain view re-runs 8s each read. Staleness contract drives the choice.

rubrics.criteria: No coherent distinction
Believes matviews auto-update or views cache
Correct choice direction; thin on CONCURRENTLY or staleness tradeoffs
Sound freshness/staleness reasoning with correct refresh mechanics

questions.explanation: Views trade compute for freshness; matviews trade freshness for compute.

questions.prompt: A booking table must forbid overlapping reservations for the same room. Compare CHECK, UNIQUE, trigger, and EXCLUSION constraint approaches; then show the declarative solution and its index requirement.
questions.reference_answer: CHECK sees one row only — cannot express pairwise non-overlap. UNIQUE prevents identical keys, not ranges. A trigger works but is hand-maintained and race-prone under concurrency. The declarative answer: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, span WITH &&) — requires a GiST index on the range; every write checks operator-satisfaction against existing rows atomically.

rubrics.criteria: Claims CHECK or UNIQUE can express it
Proposes a trigger only, with no concern for races
Identifies exclusion constraints; syntax approximate
Correct elimination of CHECK/UNIQUE, trigger tradeoff, and exact EXCLUDE syntax+index

questions.explanation: Exclusion constraints are PostgreSQL's declarative answer to pairwise row rules.

questions.prompt: Your team repeats CHECK (email ~ '.+@.+') on six tables. Design the domain-based refactor, explain what CREATE DOMAIN buys you over repeated CHECKs, and its limits (e.g., where domain constraints don't fire).
questions.reference_answer: CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '.+@.+') centralizes the rule — every column typed email inherits it; ALTER DOMAIN changes it in one place. Limits: domain checks fire on assignment, but casts/comparisons treat the value as the base type; planner ignores the constraint for estimates; constraints on domains can't reference other rows anyway.

rubrics.criteria: Proposes enum or lookup table for format checks
Knows syntax only; sees it as identical to CHECK
Correct domain mechanics; limits vague
Correct refactor, central-maintenance rationale and honest limits

questions.explanation: Domains are the DRY tool for per-type invariants — reuse, not duplication.

questions.prompt: Explain surrogate keys (identity/serial) vs natural keys for a 'users' table (email is a candidate key). Cover join cost, churn, uniqueness semantics and when exposing the surrogate publicly is a mistake.
questions.reference_answer: Surrogate bigint ids are compact join keys, stable, and opaque — but add no real-world meaning; the natural key still needs a UNIQUE constraint to prevent duplicate emails. Natural PKs save an index but leak business data and break on key churn (email change). Publicly sequential surrogates leak enumeration — pair with UUID for public exposure if needed.

rubrics.criteria: Believes surrogate removes the need for unique email enforcement
Dogmatic either direction without reasoning
Correct surrogate advantages; misses natural-key churn or uniqueness semantics
Balanced tradeoff analysis incl. the still-needed unique constraint and enumeration issue

questions.explanation: Surrogate for joins + unique constraint on the natural key is the usual settlement.

questions.prompt: Design the transaction boundaries for 'transfer funds between two accounts' (read balances, debit A, credit B, write audit log). Cover atomicity needs, savepoint use, isolation choice and what happens if the process dies mid-transaction.
questions.reference_answer: All four writes in one transaction — atomicity makes partial transfer impossible. Isolation: Read Committed suffices if balance checks happen under SELECT FOR UPDATE locks on the account rows; a race on the balance check is prevented by row locks not snapshot level. On crash, in-flight WAL/transaction state rolls back — no half-transfers. Savepoints could isolate optional steps (audit retry) without aborting the whole transfer.

rubrics.criteria: Believes a crash leaves partial commits
Thinks each statement needs its own transaction or none does
Correct atomicity requirement; isolation/lock reasoning shallow
Correct single-transaction boundary, row-lock vs isolation reasoning, crash semantics

questions.explanation: Atomicity is a property you design — group the writes that must live or die together.

questions.prompt: Explain ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ('upsert') semantics: how PostgreSQL picks the conflicting row, what EXCLUDED means, why concurrent inserts don't error, and when MERGE is the better fit.
questions.reference_answer: ON CONFLICT (col) proposes each row for insert; a violation on the inferred unique index switches to DO UPDATE on the existing row, with EXCLUDED referring to the would-be-inserted row. The speculative-insert path resolves races atomically — no lost updates under concurrency. MERGE suits multi-condition source-driven merges; ON CONFLICT is the simpler idempotent write.

rubrics.criteria: Cannot describe conflict target inference
Thinks ON CONFLICT swallows all errors
Correct upsert mechanics; unclear on concurrency or MERGE comparison
Correct conflict-target, EXCLUDED semantics, race handling and MERGE distinction

questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT is the single-statement idempotent write — MERGE is the multi-action engine.

questions.prompt: Design least-privilege roles for: an app that reads/writes business tables, a reporting tool that reads them, and migrations that alter schema. Cover role hierarchy, default privileges and why the app shouldn't own its tables.
questions.reference_answer: app_rw: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on schema tables; reporting_ro: SELECT only; migrator: owns objects/DDL. App connects as app_rw — an SQL injection can damage data but not drop tables or grant rights. Default privileges on the migrator auto-grant app_rw/reporting_ro rights on future objects. Inheritance via GRANT role TO role; NOINHERIT where step-up should be explicit.

rubrics.criteria: Believes GRANT ALL is required for the app
Single shared superuser-ish design
Reasonable role split; misses ownership or default privileges
Correct role split, ownership reasoning and default-privilege automation

questions.explanation: Ownership is itself a privilege — keep DDL power out of the application's role.

questions.prompt: Explain why marking a function SECURITY DEFINER requires extra care: whose rights it runs with, the search_path injection attack, and the safe pattern (explicit SET search_path, input validation).
questions.reference_answer: SECURITY DEFINER runs as the function owner — a controlled privilege-elevation primitive. Attack: unqualified object names inside the body resolve along the caller's search_path; a malicious user could shadow objects in a schema they control appearing earlier in the path. Safe pattern: SET search_path = '' (or a pinned list) in the function, qualify names, validate inputs, keep the owner minimal-privileged.

rubrics.criteria: Believes SECURITY DEFINER is just a firewall for SQL injection
Vague 'it is risky' without the mechanism
Knows rights elevate; misses the search_path vector or fix
Owner-context explanation, search_path attack and the correct hardening pattern

questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER is delegation — pin search_path or the delegate can be impersonated.

questions.prompt: When is a trigger the right integrity tool and when is it the wrong one? Compare triggers with constraints and generated columns for: cross-row checks, audit columns, default computation, and cascade logic. Include statement vs row granularity and performance.
questions.reference_answer: Constraints are declarative, optimizer-visible, race-free — use them first (CHECK, FK, EXCLUDE). Generated columns replace simple per-row compute triggers. Triggers fit: cross-row rules beyond exclusion constraints, auditing NEW/OLD, complex cascades, INSTEAD OF view writes. Row triggers fire per row (n×cost on bulk); statement triggers + transition tables batch better. Triggers are procedural — easy to write bugs that fire under concurrency.

rubrics.criteria: Avoids triggers categorically without reasons
Uses triggers for everything
Correct triggers-vs-constraints instinct; light on granularity/performance
Sound decision matrix with granularity and concurrency performance reasoning

questions.explanation: Declarative first, generated columns second, triggers last — but indispensable when they fit.

questions.prompt: Explain the PL/pgSQL exception model: where errors can be caught, what a BEGIN..EXCEPTION block costs (subtransaction), what FOUND is after different statements, and one correct use for 'INSERT or handle conflict'.
questions.reference_answer: EXCEPTION WHEN condition THEN catches matching SQLSTATE-class errors in the enclosing block; the block rolls back to its start — internally a subtransaction (not free on hot paths). FOUND reflects the last statement (rows for DML/SELECT INTO/FOR, performed for PERFORM/EXECUTE). The pre-v15 idempotent insert: BEGIN INSERT ... EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN NULL; END — today ON CONFLICT is cleaner.

rubrics.criteria: Cannot describe the block structure
Thinks exceptions are free or unbounded
Correct exception flow; misses FOUND or cost detail
Correct catch semantics + subtransaction cost + FOUND + valid example

questions.explanation: Exception blocks are subtransactions — expressive, but not free in tight loops.

questions.prompt: The planner chooses a catastrophic nested-loop join on a correlated (city, state) predicate pair. Explain why single-column statistics fail here, what extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) fixes, and how you'd confirm the fix.
questions.reference_answer: The planner multiplies per-column selectivities assuming independence — correlated columns (city implies state) make the estimate orders of magnitude low → nested loop over millions. CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON city, state gives the planner the joint distribution; ANALYZE then records it. Confirm: EXPLAIN ANALYZE rows≈actual and the plan flips to hash/bitmap.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests disabling nested loops as the fix
Blames indexes not estimates
Knows stats are wrong; unsure which extended stats type or verification
Independence-assumption diagnosis, correct extended-statistics fix, verification method

questions.explanation: Bad plans are often good planners fed bad statistics — fix the input, not the symptom.

questions.prompt: Defend or refute: 'A multicolumn index on (a, b) makes a redundant single-column index on (a) unnecessary.' Include leftmost-prefix reasoning, the caveat for queries on b alone, and write-cost considerations.
questions.reference_answer: Largely true: B-tree (a,b) orders by a first — equality/ranges on a alone use it efficiently, so a separate (a) index is redundant. Caveat: queries on b alone can't use (a,b) well (b is unordered within a-groups); and every index costs write/space — keeping both duplicates overhead. The reverse is not true: (a) does not serve (a,b) queries optimally.

rubrics.criteria: Believes more indexes always help
Thinks any multicolumn index helps any column subset equally
Correct on (a) redundancy; misses b-only caveat
Correct leftmost-prefix reasoning both directions + write-cost note

questions.explanation: Index design is prefix algebra — order your keys to cover the query shapes you actually run.

questions.prompt: An ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a hot 200M-row table must ship without downtime. Explain what a naive ALTER does (rewrite + ACCESS EXCLUSIVE), and the staged-migration pattern that avoids it (add column, dual-write/backfill, validate, swap).
questions.reference_answer: A type change that alters storage forces a full table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — minutes of full outage. Pattern: ADD COLUMN new (metadata-only or cheap default), deploy dual-write or trigger, backfill in batches, validate, then swap names/redirect reads and drop old — possibly with NOT VALID constraint + VALIDATE to shorten locks. REINDEX/validations still need care on hot tables.

rubrics.criteria: Proposes doing it 'at night' without addressing the rewrite
Thinks all ALTERs are instant or all need downtime equally
Knows it locks; partial migration pattern
Correct lock/rewrite mechanics and a workable staged-migration sequence

questions.explanation: Schema evolution on hot tables is a deployment pattern, not a single DDL statement.

questions.prompt: Explain search_path resolution: where unqualified names are sought, which schemas are implicitly searched, the security implications of a hostile schema on the path (especially for SECURITY DEFINER functions), and how to pin it.
questions.reference_answer: Unqualified names resolve left-to-right through search_path ($user then public by default); pg_catalog is searched implicitly unless listed. Creation lands in the first valid schema. Risk: if an attacker can create objects in a schema earlier on someone's path (or shadow built-ins), unqualified calls pick theirs — critical in SECURITY DEFINER context. Fix: SET search_path explicitly per role/function and qualify names.

rubrics.criteria: Thinks path order is alphabetical or global
Knows search_path exists; no security reasoning
Correct resolution; vague on the security angle
Correct resolution order, implicit catalog, attack mechanism and remediation

questions.explanation: search_path is a name-resolution chain — every unqualified name is a security decision.

questions.prompt: timestamptz vs timestamp: design guidance for an events table in a multi-timezone product. Cover what each stores, how session TimeZone changes output, interval arithmetic pitfalls (DST), and a schema recommendation.
questions.reference_answer: timestamptz stores an absolute instant (UTC internally) — correct for 'when did it happen'; display follows session TimeZone. timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no zone meaning — correct for '3pm local at the store' schedules. Pitfall: adding interval '1 day' across DST changes absolute vs calendar semantics differently per type. Recommendation: timestamptz + store reporting zones separately.

rubrics.criteria: Cannot distinguish the types
Thinks timestamptz stores the zone
Correct basic storage difference; shallow on DST/session semantics
Absolute-instant vs wall-clock distinction, zone-display behavior, DST-aware reasoning, sound recommendation

questions.explanation: timestamptz is for instants; timestamp is for unanchored wall-clocks — most 'times' are instants.

questions.prompt: A jsonb 'attrs' column supports arbitrary facet search (color, size...). Explain containment query + GIN indexing, jsonb_path_ops vs jsonb_ops tradeoff, and when an EAV relational design or generated columns + B-tree beats jsonb.
questions.reference_answer: attrs @> '{"color":"red"}' uses GIN: jsonb_ops indexes all keys/values supporting @>, ?, ?|, ?&; jsonb_path_ops is smaller/faster but only supports @> (and jsonpath). At scale with hot facets, generated columns extracting keys + B-tree or a real EAV/attribute table gives better selectivity and typed predicates; jsonb wins on schema flexibility.

rubrics.criteria: Believes jsonb queries are always fastest
Thinks jsonb can't be indexed or needs full scans
Correct GIN support; misses path_ops or alternatives
Correct GIN mechanics, path_ops tradeoff and honest alternatives

questions.explanation: jsonb+GIN is real infrastructure — but typed columns still beat it on hot paths.

questions.prompt: An org-chart closure query must return all descendants of a node. Explain how WITH RECURSIVE evaluation works (working table, iteration, termination), why cyclic hierarchies break naive queries, and the two fixes (UNION vs CYCLE clause).
questions.reference_answer: The non-recursive term seeds the working table; each iteration joins new rows into the CTE until an empty iteration ends it. A cycle (a→b→a) without dedup loops forever. UNION (not ALL) deduplicates rows — cycles terminate but duplicates also die (correct for sets of nodes). The CYCLE clause marks repeated paths and stops re-expansion — better when path shape matters; SEARCH orders traversal depth/breadth.

rubrics.criteria: Thinks recursion needs a LIMIT to be safe
Can write a recursive CTE but not explain termination
Correct mechanics; only one cycle fix or shaky on UNION vs CYCLE
Accurate iteration model + both cycle defenses with their tradeoffs

questions.explanation: Recursive CTEs are graph traversal in SQL — termination is a property you must design for.

questions.prompt: Explain transaction ID wraparound: what XIDs are, why 32 bits forces recycling, what 'freezing' does, and what happens operationally if a database approaches wraparound (including why autovacuum can't be fully switched off).
questions.reference_answer: Every transaction consumes a 32-bit XID (~4B); visibility compares ages relative to current XID — after ~2B transactions the comparison wraps and old committed tuples would look 'future'. VACUUM freezes old tuples (marks them always-visible) before the horizon. Ignoring wraparound forces PostgreSQL into emergency aggressive vacuum, then shutdown-protection mode — hence autovacuum's mandatory role.

rubrics.criteria: Believes XIDs never exhaust or that restart resets them
Mentions wraparound exists; mechanism wrong
Understands wraparound risk; imprecise on freezing or the emergency behavior
XID arithmetic, freeze mechanism, and operational consequences correct

questions.explanation: Wraparound is why VACUUM is not optional — it is existential maintenance.

questions.prompt: Explain the write-ahead logging rule, what happens on a crash between 'data page written' and 'commit record flushed', and how checkpoints bound recovery work.
questions.reference_answer: WAL rule: a change's log record must reach stable storage before the data page it describes. On crash, recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint — a commit whose record never flushed is simply absent (rolled back logically). Checkpoints flush dirty pages so replay only needs WAL after them; they trade burst I/O for bounded crash-recovery time.

rubrics.criteria: Believes data pages must be written first
Knows WAL exists; cannot reason about the crash window
Understands replay; fuzzy on checkpoint mechanics or the crash edge case
Log-first rule, crash scenario semantics, checkpoint role all correct

questions.explanation: Durability comes from ordering: log first, data later — crash recovery is 'replay the log'.

questions.prompt: shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem: explain what each bounds, why work_mem×nodes can exceed expectations, and a safe-first-tuning approach for a 16GB dedicated server.
questions.reference_answer: shared_buffers = the server's page cache (~25% RAM is a sane start). work_mem = per sort/hash node — a plan with 8 sorts can use 8×; OLTP keeps it modest, reporting can raise it per-session. maintenance_work_mem = vacuum/index-build workspace (separate budget). Approach: small conservative global values, measure, raise per-workload via SET LOCAL rather than globally.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests maxing all memory to the server
Names settings without accurate roles
Correct buffer/work_mem distinction; multiplier detail weak
Correct semantics for all three, the multiplier hazard and a defensible first pass

questions.explanation: Memory tuning is about concurrency multipliers, not 'more is better'.

questions.prompt: Your app slows down every afternoon. Describe a monitoring workflow using pg_stat_activity (live state), pg_stat_statements (aggregate offenders), and pg_stat_user_tables (seq_scan vs idx_scan, dead tuples) to localize the cause.
questions.reference_answer: pg_stat_activity during the slowdown: find wait states, long queries, blocking chains. pg_stat_statements for the top cumulative time consumers (mean_exec_time×calls) — separates 'always slow' from 'afternoon storms'. pg_stat_user_tables reveals seq_scan-heavy hot tables needing indexes and n_dead_tup growth needing vacuum tuning. Correlate with cron/batch jobs overlapping the window.

rubrics.criteria: Proposes random fixes without data
Only 'check slow queries' generically
Uses two views correctly
Uses all three views with the right diagnostic questions

questions.explanation: Diagnosis sequence: what runs now (activity) → what costs most overall (statements) → what tables suffer (stats).

questions.prompt: Design full-text search for a support-ticket system: tsvector column population (generated column vs trigger), the config/language choice, GIN indexing, query-side tsquery variants, and headline/ranking basics.
questions.reference_answer: Store a generated tsvector column from title+body (to_tsvector('english', ...)) or maintain via trigger; use a fixed dictionary config so lexemes are stable. GIN index on the vector. Query side: plainto_tsquery for free text, to_tsquery for boolean control, websearch_to_tsquery for user syntax; @@ matches, ts_rank orders; ts_headline renders snippets.

rubrics.criteria: Suggests regex scanning per query
Basic LIKE-level thinking without tsvector
Correct tsvector/tsquery + GIN; missing population or ranking detail
Complete pipeline: population, config stability, GIN, query functions, ranking

questions.explanation: FTS is a pipeline (document→vector→index→query→rank), not a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: Your LEFT JOIN 'loses' unmatched rows after you add WHERE r.status='active'. Explain the bug precisely (evaluation order vs NULL padding), give the correct rewrite, and when the WHERE-form is actually intended.
questions.reference_answer: LEFT JOIN pads unmatched right columns with NULL; a WHERE on r.* filters those padded rows out — recreating an inner join. Fix: put the predicate in the ON clause (filter the right side before padding) or make it NULL-tolerant. The WHERE form is correct only when you genuinely want inner-join semantics — then write INNER JOIN for clarity.

rubrics.criteria: Cannot reproduce the issue
Blames the join not the predicate placement
Identifies the bug class; fix imprecise
Explains padding+WHERE interaction exactly and gives the ON-clause fix

questions.explanation: Predicate placement (ON vs WHERE) changes outer-join semantics — the classic bug.

questions.prompt: Compare CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF and GREATEST/LEAST for: defaulting a column, guarding division, mapping codes to labels, and clamping to a range. For each, give the idiomatic choice and one misuse to avoid.
questions.reference_answer: Default → COALESCE (first non-null chain). Division guard → NULLIF (x/NULLIF(y,0)). Code mapping → CASE (readable branches; simple CASE for equality). Clamp → GREATEST/LEAST (PG's NULL-ignoring semantics — beware assuming NULL propagation). Misuses: CASE re-evaluating volatile expressions per branch; COALESCE evaluating a subquery twice vs NULLIF clarity; GREATEST on all-NULL rows giving NULL.

rubrics.criteria: Invents functions or wrong signatures
Interchangeable view of the four
Mostly right tool choices; misses GREATEST NULL semantics or a misuse
Right tool per job with correct PostgreSQL-specific NULL semantics and a real misuse each

questions.explanation: Each conditional has an idiom — pick the one that says what you mean.

questions.prompt: name LIKE 'Jo%' is fast but '%son' is not — explain left-anchored vs contains matching and B-tree index usage, what ILIKE changes for indexes, and the escape rules. Mention pg_trgm as the contains alternative.
questions.reference_answer: 'Jo%' is a left-anchored prefix — a B-tree on name can range-scan the prefix interval (collation caveat: needs C-locale-style ops or text_pattern_ops for LIKE). '%son' has no anchor — full scan. ILIKE doesn't change indexability (expression index on lower(name) helps). pg_trgm GIN indexes trigram similarity enabling contains/regex searches.

rubrics.criteria: No understanding of index selectivity
Thinks all LIKE uses indexes
Knows prefix searches index better; misses trgm or ILIKE nuance
Anchoring/index mechanics correct + ILIKE + trigram alternative

questions.explanation: Indexes need left edges — 'contains' searches need a different index structure.

questions.prompt: When is a text[] column better than a child table for multi-valued attributes (e.g. product tags)? Cover query/unnest ergonomics, GIN indexing, ordering/uniqueness semantics and the normalization tradeoff.
questions.reference_answer: Arrays fit small bounded lists queried as sets — unnest explodes for analysis, @>+GIN gives membership search, no join needed. Lost: per-element foreign keys, uniqueness constraints, ordering guarantees, per-element updates, standard tooling expectations. Child table = proper modeling when elements have identity/lifecycle or need FK/UNIQUE. tags[] for simple labels; line items never in arrays.

rubrics.criteria: Thinks arrays can't be indexed
Advocates arrays everywhere or never
Knows arrays exist; partial on indexing or constraints
Correct use-case boundary with mechanics and the normalization cost

questions.explanation: Arrays are a denormalization convenience — choose them knowing exactly what integrity you gave up.

questions.prompt: When is a procedure better than a function in PostgreSQL? Cover CALL vs SELECT invocation, transaction control (COMMIT inside), return values vs OUT params, and one scenario each where each is wrong.
questions.reference_answer: Procedures run via CALL, return nothing directly (OUT params optional), and can commit/rollback mid-run — long batch jobs with periodic commits. Functions run in SELECT, return values/SETOF, cannot control transactions. Wrong uses: a procedure for a value needed in a query; a function for a job that must commit incrementally (would hold one giant transaction).

rubrics.criteria: Believes procedures are deprecated
Thinks they're interchangeable
Correct CALL/SELECT distinction; thin on transaction control
Invocation + transaction-control + return-shape distinctions with sound scenarios

questions.explanation: Functions compute inside a transaction; procedures orchestrate work across commits.

questions.prompt: Explain UNLOGGED vs TEMPORARY vs regular tables: durability, visibility, WAL overhead, lifetime semantics — and pick the right kind for an ETL staging table, a session-scratchpad, and the canonical orders table.
questions.reference_answer: Regular: WAL-logged durable shared tables — orders. UNLOGGED: skips WAL (fast writes) but truncated on crash — ETL staging where reload is cheap. TEMPORARY: session-private, optionally ON COMMIT DROP, invisible to others — per-session scratchpad; also not WAL-logged but for isolation reasons.

rubrics.criteria: Cannot match any type to a scenario
Thinks temp tables are shared or unlogged is per-session
Two of three correct; mixes visibility vs durability axes
All three distinguished correctly with matching use-cases

questions.explanation: Table durability/visibility are independent axes — pick per data lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Enum type vs lookup table for an order status field: compare storage, adding values, renaming values, foreign-key semantics, cross-schema portability and reporting-tool expectations.
questions.reference_answer: Enum: compact 4-byte storage, declared order, type-safe — but adding values needs ALTER TYPE (transaction caveats), can't be dropped per-value, and tools see an opaque type. Lookup table: FK enforcement, ON UPDATE actions, values manageable via DML, self-documenting for BI joins — costs a join/int column. Enum suits stable closed sets; lookup table for evolving business vocabularies.

rubrics.criteria: Believes lookup tables are obsolete
Only 'enums are simpler'
Correct mechanics mostly; weak decision criteria
Complete accurate comparison with a defensible decision rule

questions.explanation: Closed stable sets → enum; business-evolving vocabularies → table.

questions.prompt: Why does 'abc' + 1 fail but '10' + 5 return 15? Explain PostgreSQL's unknown-literal resolution, the difference between implicit/assignment/explicit casts, and the design risk of relying on implicit casts in application SQL.
questions.reference_answer: Unknown literals take the type context demands: + on '10' resolves it as integer; 'abc' fails integer input validation at parse/execution. Cast kinds: implicit (automatic, e.g. int→numeric), assignment (on column write), explicit (CAST/::). App risk: implicit behavior varies by context/version and hides conversions — explicit casts at boundaries make intent auditable and avoid 'it worked until the type changed'.

rubrics.criteria: Claims PostgreSQL auto-converts anything
Thinks it's magic/bug-prone without the mechanism
Understands '10'+5; fuzzy on cast categories or risk
Correct literal-resolution + cast taxonomy + the engineering risk

questions.explanation: Implicit casts are conveniences with rules — explicit intent survives schema evolution.

questions.prompt: An app serves 10k tenants via connection pooling — one DB role, many app users. Design the row-security integration: how the tenant id reaches the policy (SET LOCAL vs session GUC), transaction-scoping pitfalls in pooled transactions, and why per-request SET must be mandatory.
questions.reference_answer: Pattern: pool sets SET LOCAL app.tenant = '42' inside each transaction; policy USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int). SET LOCAL is transaction-scoped — resets at commit, safe for pooling. Pitfalls: a plain SET leaks across the pool boundary between checkouts; a transaction missing SET gets default-deny (fail closed — good). The pool middleware must guarantee the SET runs before any tenant query — a forgotten set must never return wrong-tenant data.

rubrics.criteria: Ignores the connection-pool lifecycle entirely
Proposes per-tenant DB roles for 10k tenants
Correct GUC approach; misses transaction-scoping or pooling hazard
Correct SET-LOCAL pattern, pooling lifecycle reasoning, fail-closed safety

questions.explanation: RLS + pooling works — but only if the tenant context is transaction-scoped and mandatory.
